October 6, 2013 – October 12, 2014

II

JOHN L. COOPER III

Grand Master – 2013-2014

John Cooper began his association with Freemasonry in 1958 when he
was initiated into the Order of DeMolay in Fullerton, California. He later served as
Master Councilor of his chapter, and was honored with the Degree of Chevalier
and the DeMolay Legion of Honor. He is now an Honorary Member of the
International Supreme Council of the Order of DeMolay.
He was raised a Master Mason in Azure Lodge No. 533 at Fullerton,
and later served as Master of James A. Foshay Lodge No. 641 in Los
Angeles. That lodge is now a part of Culver City – Foshay Lodge No. 467 in
Culver City. In addition, he is a member of Eureka Lodge No. 16 at Auburn,
Consuelo Lodge No. 325 at Escondido, Phoenix Lodge No. 144 and ColumbiaBrotherhood Lodge No. 370, both in San Francisco, and Burlingame Lodge
No. 400. He is a past master of both Northern California and Southern California
research lodges, and over the years has served on many Grand Lodge committees
and boards.
John is a Thirty-Third Degree Scottish Rite Mason and a Knight of
the York Grand Cross of Honor in the York Rite. He is a member of the Shrine, and
many other Masonic organizations. His interest in the history and philosophy
of Freemasonry led him to membership in many Masonic research bodies, and
he is First Vice President of the Philalethes Society – America’s oldest and largest
Masonic research organization.
He holds a bachelor’s and a master’s degree in Political Science
from the University of California, Los Angeles, and a Ph.D. in Education from
Claremont Graduate School. For twenty-five years he was a public high school
teacher and administrator, including serving five years as the superintendent of
the Escondido Union High School District in San Diego County.
In 1991 he was elected as Grand Secretary of the Masonic Grand
Lodge of California, and held that position under eighteen Grand Masters until
his retirement in 2008. John and Heather, his wife of thirty-one years, have
five children, three daughters-in-law, one son-in-law, and seven grandchildren.
They make their home in Lincoln, California, where both are active members of
the Episcopal Church.

One Hundred Sixty-Fifth
Annual Communication
Friday Afternoon, October 10, 2014
The 165th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand Master
John L. Cooper III on Friday, October 10, 2014.
Worshipful Brother Eric C. Chilson, Master of Eureka Lodge No. 16,
raised the opening session of Grand Lodge. The gavel used to raise Grand Lodge
was presented to the Grand Master by his parents when he was installed as Master
Councilor of Fullerton Chapter, Order of DeMolay, in 1961.
Reception of the Past Grand Masters
The Grand Master welcomed the brethren and directed the Grand
Marshal to present the Past Grand Masters of the Grand Lodge of California at
the Altar. The Grand Marshal then introduced each Past Grand Master, following
which the Grand Master, accompanied by the Deputy Grand Master, personally
greeted each one. The Grand Master asked the brethren to join him in saluting our
Past Grand Masters by the battery of three times three. The Past Grand Masters
were then escorted to seats reserved for them in the auditorium. The Grand Master
then directed the Grand Secretary to send to each absent Past Grand Master the
usual letter of greeting from the Grand Lodge.
Roll Call
The Grand Secretary was asked to call the roll of Grand Lodge Officers,
Past Grand Masters, and Past Grand Officers, and to ascertain if a constitutional
number were present to convene the Grand Lodge of California. The following
were present as indicated by their response to the calling of the roll:

8

Proceedings of the
Auditorium Rededication

Grand Master Cooper called on Worshipful Brother Mark Pressey,
President of the California Masonic Memorial Temple Board of Trustees for his
remarks on the renovation of the auditorium.
“Thank you, Most Worshipful. Good afternoon, brethren. Sixty years
ago when the leadership of this fraternity first conceived of the idea for the
California Masonic Memorial Temple, the main Masonic purpose for the building
was to accommodate the Annual Communication. At that time, the Grand Lodge
headquarters was on Van Ness Avenue and while it had many lodge rooms, it
did not have sufficient space for the Annual Communication. The plan for this
memorial temple was that it would be used by the Masons of California for the
Annual Communication one week out of the year and that it would be made
available to the public the rest of the year for concerts, conventions, meetings,
and special events.
Since the building first opened in 1958, millions of people have come
through its doors for one occasion or another. The first event in the building was
a concert and since then hundreds of artists have played in the venue over the
decades. Major corporations like IBM, Pacific Bell and PG&E were frequent
clients hosting special events and meetings in the building. The revenue from
these operations always sustained the building.
By the time we reached the 21st century, the building began to lose its
relevance in the community and fewer and fewer major clients were choosing
our building as the venue for their concerts and events. Revenue was not keeping
pace with the rising costs of operating the building. There were two major factors
contributing to this decline.
The first was the configuration of the stage. You might remember that it
was a long and narrow stage – called a thrust stage. While many clients liked the
intimacy the stage provided, it no longer fit their business model. The technical
aspects, like the sound and lighting, for most concerts and major events are preprogrammed for the more traditional stage known as a proscenium stage, which
is wide and not as deep as the thrust stage. CMMT was losing good clients
that did not want to bring in different equipment and re-program their event to
accommodate the thrust stage.
The second issue was the fixed configuration of the main floor. Events
planners and concert promoters today have grown accustomed to having a variety
of options for the room setup, which includes conference style, theater style,
classroom style, and styles for receptions and banquets. Concerts today are both
seated and non-seated. The fixed nature of our auditorium prohibited the flexibility
that good clients desired.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

9

So the CMMT created a plan to fix these two issues and revitalize the
use of the building. We now have a proscenium stage that is sixty feet wide and
thirty-six feet deep – matching the industry standards for almost any occasion. We
have added a sixteen-foot extension to the stage to accommodate our ceremonies
this weekend. We also removed the fixed seats on the main floor and created four
tiers of level flooring. In this new configuration we can accommodate all types
of seating options for concerts and we can provide conference style and theater
style seating. We can do a reception for 1800 people and a seated banquet for 800.
The Masons of California will utilize the banquet setup next year when the Friday
night banquet and entertainment for World Conference of Regular Grand Lodges
will be held in this auditorium. In addition, we added a new, state of the art sound
and lighting system; we upgraded the concourse, the backstage rooms, and the
California Room.
The CMMT also sought and found a single operator for the building
with a single food and beverage operator. Having a single operator, rather than
renting the facility to a new operator for each event, provides a much higher
level of consistency and accountability in the operation of the building. These
arrangements also provide consistent and regularly increasing income to the
CMMT. CMMT entered into a long–term lease with Live Nation Entertainment
who now manages the operation of the building.
The renovated auditorium officially opened on September 17 to rave
reviews by the press, meeting planners, and concert promoters. Live Nation has
a full calendar of concerts scheduled in the building along with corporate events
with clients like Oracle, Salesforce, Apple and others.
As a result of these renovations, together with these new partnerships,
the financial future for the CMMT is bright and our Memorial Temple is a vibrant,
relevant, valued asset in the community once again.
Thank you, Most Worshipful.”
Grand Master Cooper thanked Brother Pressey and the board of trustees
for their vision and leadership on the renovation project.
Grand Master Cooper then directed attention to the video screen for a
presentation on the new staircase, handcrafted by Worshipful Brother Christopher
Holme, after which the Grand Lodge officers performed a rededication ceremony.
The Grand Chaplain offered the following invocation:
“Great Architect and Ruler of the Universe! We most reverently invoke
Thy blessing on this memorable occasion. We remember and thank Thee, for the
vision of our Brethren, who pledged their faith, dedication and integrity to the

renovation and revitalization of this auditorium. May the pledges of our Brethren

this edifice. And to thee we shall ascribe all the honor and glory forever. Amen.”

After delivering his Decisions, the Grand Master resumed his station and

Video Presentation
The Grand Lodge of California premiered a new video entitled “The Art
of Masonic Education.” From floor sketches to tracing boards, Masonic artists
over the centuries have produced incredible works to serve as lodge teaching aids.
In addition to being artifacts of our fraternity, many of these pieces are treasures
of the art world. This video explores the history and significance of art in Masonic
education from the 18th century to today, as told by historians, Masonic scholars,
and some of the artists themselves.

refreshment, to be called on again at 8:30 a.m. on Saturday, October 11.

15

Memorial Service
The Grand Master called on the Very Reverend Leonard B. Oakes, Grand
Chaplain, to present a service of remembrance for our departed brethren.
One of the greatest miracles that we can do as people of God when the
kind messenger gently translates one of our love ones from this imperfect, to that
all perfect lodge above where the supreme grand master of the universe forever
presides, is our availability to come together, comfort and lighten the burden of
each other. In that experience, we then begin to accept that part of our lives will
have to go and that our hope to meet them again will be realized when that time
comes where we too, are being called to join them, there in that heavenly realm
where everlasting love reigns.
You see, dying is a gradual diminishing and final vanishing over the
horizon of life. It is like that ship bound for Utopia leaving a port and moving
toward the horizon. In our very eyes, it becomes smaller and smaller until we
can no longer see it. But if we only trust that someone is standing on a faraway
shore seeing that that same ship becomes larger and larger until it reaches its new
harbor, and when we trust that God is standing at the other shore eagerly waiting
to welcome our beloved ones into a new home, a smile can break through our
tears. Yes, a smile will soothe our sorrows and be thankful.
Life, however short it may be, is like a bucket with rocks, pebbles and
sand in it. The rocks are the important things, your family, your spouse, your
health, your children. Things that if everything else was lost and only they
remained, your life would still be complete.
The pebbles are the other things that matter. Like your job, your house,
your security, your car, your golf club membership.
The sand is everything else, the small things.
If you put the sand into the bucket first, there is no room for the pebbles
or the rocks. The same goes for your life. If you spend all your time and energy on
the small stuff, you will never have room for the things that are important to you.
Things that money can’t buy, such as quality time with your family.
Pay attention to the things that are critical to your happiness. Play with
your children and grandchildren. Take your spouse, partners, parents, family and
friend out for a date, into the ballpark or your favorite places. There will always be
time to go to work, clean the house, give a dinner party, play golf, or do gardening.
“Take care of the rocks first, the things that really matter. Set your
priorities. The rest is just sand.”
Let us all keep the basic unit of our lives, our family, for to each other, we
grow in strength and love on our journey to meet God face to face.

Proceedings of the
I pray for courage and hope for the Grand Lodge of California
family. Time, patience and perseverance will accomplish all
things. Healing will come when we trust that God will continue
to lift us up from such pain and hurt. We all live and we all
die. May we all live with purpose, and die accomplishing those
purposes. So that when we come to meet our maker, there shall
be no doubt, there shall be no fear, but with a report full of
smile. Yes, when that time comes, we shall be reunited with
those whom we love. Don’t give up yet, said those who have
been there on the other side, and you are surrounded by many
of them, they say, “Don’t give up!! Stay the race until you reach
the finish line, for there God commanded life, even life forever
more. Amen.

Most Worshipful Harry L. Maynard, Past Grand Master, delivered a
eulogy for the late Past Grand Master, Donald G. Ingalls.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

17

Eulogy
Donald George Ingalls
Most Worshipful Donald G. Ingalls entered into the Celestial Lodge
Above at the age of 95 on March 10, 2014, after a long illness in Olympia,
Washington. He was born July 29, 1918, to Park Ingalls and Luella “LuLu”
Morris Ingalls in Humboldt, Nebraska. He lived an unassuming, but quite
remarkable life.
Don considered Stafford, Kansas his happy childhood home, despite
harsh economic conditions. He returned to visit as often as possible. He moved
to Southern California with his mother in the 1930s. There he attended North
Hollywood High School while working at various menial jobs to help support
the family.
He attended George Washington University, located in Washington, D.C.,
and graduated with a degree of Bachelor of Arts in English. His post-graduate
studies in English literature and philosophy were completed at the University of
Southern California in Los Angeles.
During World War II, our Past Grand Master served in the United States
Army Air Corps and was assigned to the European theater of operations. After
the close of this war, and until 1957, he was an engineering test pilot for North
American Aviation, a columnist and reporter for the Washington Post and then a
public information officer for the Los Angeles Police Department.
A writer since childhood, Don wrote freelance for publications such as
Desert Magazine. He was a columnist for “The Valley Times” in North Hollywood,
and was editor of “The Beat” magazine for the LAPD.
It was there he formed a friendship with fellow police officer Gene
Rodenberry, later the creator of Star Trek. Eventually both men transitioned to the
burgeoning television industry where Don spent over 35 years as a prolific film
and television writer and producer.
In this capacity, he was accorded writing honors from The Writers’ Guild
of America, The National Council of Churches, The Western Writers of America
and The Academy of Television Arts and Sciences. Many national television
network shows were written and others produced by this creative Mason. During
his Hollywood career, Don wrote and produced for numerous highly regarded
TV series, such as “Have Gun, Will Travel,” “Bonanza,” “The Big Valley,” “The
Virginian,” “Gunsmoke,” “Marcus Welby, M.D.,” “Star Trek,” “Police Story” and
“Fantasy Island.” He also wrote the feature film, “Airport 1975,” along with TV
films, such as “Captain America” and “The Initiation of Sarah.”

18

Proceedings of the

On retiring to Olympia, Washington in 1987, Don wrote a novel, “The
Watchers on the Mountain.” As a man of abiding faith, he enthusiastically used
his talents for his church, writing many skits, directing children in puppetry and
drama, and writing a stage play for Westwood Baptist Church. He also mentored
and encouraged younger writers.
Don was raised a Master Mason on July 31, 1948 in North Hollywood
Lodge No. 542. He served that Lodge as Master in 1958 and in 1961 affiliated
with Hollywood Lodge No. 355 as a plural member. In 1969, he demitted from
Hollywood Lodge No. 355 and affiliated with San Buenaventura Lodge No. 214
as a plural member.
He served as the 113th Grand Master of California and Hawaii in 197879. During his term, Don truly exemplified and forcefully demonstrated that
Masonry is a “Willingness of the Heart.” His professional abilities enabled him
to express in stirring words the depth of his knowledge and his strong convictions
in Masonic matters, thus inspiring all who were privileged to hear his impressive
messages. In recognition of his outstanding writing and oratorical abilities he was
appointed Grand Orator of the Grand Lodge of California in 1974, serving under
Grand Master Burton Meyer, Jr. The following year, he was elected Junior Grand
Warden. He was also made Knight Commander, Court of Honor by the Supreme
Council, Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite and was the proud recipient of the
DeMolay Legion of Honor Award.
While Chairman of the Grand Lodge Films and Creative Projects
Committee, Don produced three Masonic films, which were viewed not only
by many Lodges and groups in this Jurisdiction, but in many of our Sister
Jurisdictions as well. Each of these films received high praise as capturing the
flavor and essence of the spirit of Masonry.
As Grand Master, Brother Ingalls helped in establishing the first Masonic
Congress of the Three Californias: California, Baja California North and Baja
California South. He was also instrumental in achieving recognition by our Grand
Lodge of the Grand Lodge of Baja California South.
Few Masons have ever contributed more to the support of our public
schools system. Grand Master Ingalls, in his travels throughout the Jurisdiction,
continually spoke on behalf of public education, emphasizing the importance of
this concept and the role it has played in a free and democratic society.
Three significant honors were bestowed upon our outstanding brother
during his term as Grand Master. He was invited to deliver the keynote address
at the Grand Masters’ Conference of North America, held in Colorado Springs,
Colorado. He was also appointed as Chairman of the Grand Masters Conference
of North America Committee to plan the program to honor the 250th anniversary
of the birth of George Washington, held in February 1982.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

19

The third and perhaps most significant honor he received was bestowed
upon him by the Grand Lodge Nationale of France, that of Honorary Past Grand
Senior Warden, the highest honor which can be given to a non French citizen. He
was also elected dual member of Stability/Concorde Lodge No. 29/42 located in
Paris, France. This latter honor, along with his friendships established with Baja
California North and South, bear witness to the way in which Most Worshipful
Don embodied the universality of Masonry.
Don is survived by Mary, his wife of almost 49 years, and daughter
Lori Harasta, son-in-law Jim Harasta and two grandchildren, Nicole and Logan
Harasta. He is also survived by first wife, Annie Smith Ingalls, daughter Diana
Ingalls-Farrell, and son-in-law Thomas “Nick” Farrell. He is also remembered by
niece Norma Stemple and her sons, grandchildren, and great grandchildren, and
by the six children of his niece Marvel Lee Richardson.
There is no question this creative, talented and acclaimed man and
true Mason will be missed by us all, and that his memory will continue to be
a blessing. Inspired by the leadership and wisdom of such men as Donald G.
Ingalls, Masonry will continue to be a source of strength in our world, enriching
all of us by its new dimension.

Proceedings of the

Very Worshipful Glenn D. Woody, Past Grand Treasurer, delivered a
eulogy for the late Past Grand Master, Vernon Leon Gordon.

Eulogy
Vernon Leon Gordon
Vernon Leon Gordon, Farmer and Past Grand Master Born on June 10,
1928 in Bixby, Oklahoma. Entered into rest on January 9, 2014, age 85 years.
Vernon was the epitome of the self-made, self-educated man. His formal
education ended in the 10th grade, when at age 15, he left home to fend for himself.
And fend he did.
He made his way to California’s San Joaquin Valley. His various jobs
included working in a grocery store/gasoline station, chopping cotton, working 12
hour all-night shifts irrigating cotton for $1 per night, setting pins in the bowling
alley for 2 cents a line, making and selling popcorn at the local theatre, serving as
the projectionist at the theatre, milking cows, bailing and hauling hay, becoming
the head pressman at the cotton gin, and driving a gasoline truck. In addition, he
served a tour of duty in the United States Air Force before turning to farming.
He met Flora Mae Reese in Tranquillity, California. She was heard to
say, “I hope that Vernon Gordon asks me out so I can tell him NO”. He did, and
she did. But, she eventually said, “Yes”. They were married in the Methodist
Church in Tranquillity in 1950, and had 64 years together. They had two adopted
children, Sarah and David and two grandchildren, Caitlin and David, Jr.
Vernon started farming with his father-in-law in 1950, and retired in the
year 2000, after 50 years. It was truly said that “he was an expert in his field”.
He was very civic-minded, serving on various Boards and Committees
of the local telephone company, the West Hills College (where he was awarded
an Honorary Degree for his service), the Tranquillity Methodist Church and
many others. Among his many tributes was being named Tranquillity Citizen of
the Year.
Vernon’s service to the Masonic Family was varied and extensive. He
joined Joppa Lodge No. 508 (now Madera No. 280) in 1956, on the same night
as his father-in-law and served as Worshipful Master in 1961 and again in 1965.
He served as an Inspector, Assistant Grand Lecturer and on many Grand Lodge
Boards and Committees, before serving as Grand Master of Masons in California
and Hawaii in 1980.
Vernon was active in Eastern Star, serving as Worthy Patron several
times and as Worthy Grand Patron in California in 1992. He served as Executive
Officer of the Northern California DeMolay Association and was awarded the
Grand Cross of Color by the International Order of Rainbow for Girls.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

23

He was active in the Fresno Valley Scottish Rite, was awarded the 33rd
Degree Honorary in 1977 and served as Personal Representative in that Valley.
Vernon had a quick wit and was always ready with a joke, a quip, a
quotation, a poem, a Bible passage, an invocation, or a sermon. As an example, on
one occasion at a Lodge dinner, he was asked to give the invocation and with less
than a minute’s advance notice, he delivered a most appropriate prayer in perfect
rhyming verse, something he obviously had tucked away in his memory for just
such an occasion.
At the 50th wedding anniversary celebration for his Grand Marshal,
Gordon Vaughan and his wife Gwen, Vernon’s toast to Brother Vaughan, after
observing a lot of hugging going on, was, “T’wood be a sad, sad day for the lady
if the men should find her charmless, but it is a sadder day yet for the gentleman,
my Brother, when the ladies all find him harmless”.
Most Worshipful Brother Gordon’s gentle, caring and kind nature is
sorely missed and his devotion to his family, his community, his friends, his
Masonic Brothers and his Masonry is something we should all emulate.
Rest in Peace, my Brother.

Most Worshipful M. William Holsinger, Past Grand Master, delivered a
eulogy for the late Past Grand Master, Stanley Lyall Channon.

Eulogy
Stanley Lyall Channon
Most Worshipful Stanley L. Channon was born in Australia, where he
grew up and earned his Bachelor’s Degree. He then moved to America to continue
his education. He completed his Master’s Degree at The University of Utah, and
a PhD in Metallurgical Engineering at The University of Illinois. His professional
career involved metallurgical research and development in aluminum, titanium,
magnesium, beryllium, steel fabrication and composite materials, and management
of aerospace technology teams. He served Aerospace Corporation for 17 years as
Manager of the Materials Division. He and his wife, Elizabeth, left their Riverside
home and moved to Washington, D.C. for three years where he conducted a
world-wide analysis of the status of metallurgical technology as a consultant to
the Pentagon.
He earned the Australian equivalent of Eagle Scout and eventually
became a Cub Master, and later Scout Master of Troup #112 in Riverside. He
earned his private pilot license under the guidance of his son Bryon, now a
commercial airline pilot.
Stan became a member of Evergreen Lodge No. 259 in Riverside in
1959, and served as Master in 1965. For twelve years he served as Inspector of
the old 616th District. During my own year as Master of Evergreen Lodge in
1971, I appointed Stan Chairman of the Evergreen Lodge Building Committee
where he supervised the design, construction, and dedication of the Evergreen
Masonic Center.
In 1983 he was appointed a Trustee of the Masonic Homes of California,
and served as Chairman of the expansion program at both homes from 1985 to
1989. This provided a 120 bed skilled nursing building, the new Siminoff Center
with Chapel and Lodge Room, a new Administrator’s residence at Union City as
well as a 56 unit adult apartment complex and social center at Covina.
He was elected Junior Grand Warden in 1985, and Grand Master of
Masons in California and Hawaii in 1988. As Grand Master he oversaw the
formation of the Grand Lodge of Hawaii, and had the pleasure of installing its
first corps of officers.
From 1993 until 2001, Stan chaired the Tournament of Roses Parade
Float Committee raising funds, designing and overseeing construction of “The
Family of Freemasonry” floats. Many of these floats received awards from the
Pasadena Tournament of Roses Association.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

25

Most Worshipful Stan was a Past President of the Southern California
Past Master Association, a 33rd Degree member of Scottish Rite, a member of
the York Rite Bodies, two Shrine Temples, the Red Cross of Constantine, the
Royal Order of Scotland, the Robert the Bruce Association, and the Riverside
High Twelve Club.
When Stan and his devoted wife, Beth, moved to Valley Springs, he
affiliated with Calaveras Lodge No. 78 in San Andreas where he chaired their
150-year Celebration Committee.
Stan was an organizer, a tireless worker, and could always be counted on
for a joke or two.
In addition to his wife, Beth, Stan leaves his daughter, Nancy, and two
sons, John and Bryan. John is also a Past Master of Evergreen Lodge No. 259
and currently serves as Inspector of the 822nd Masonic District, which includes
Evergreen Lodge just as his father before him.
In contemplating the distinguished life of Stanley Channon I am
reminded of a Hebrew proverb which admonishes us to “say not in grief that he is
no more, but say in thankfulness that he was.”

Proceedings of the

Most Worshipful David R. Doan, Past Grand Master, delivered a eulogy
for the late Past Grand Master, Allen Brooks Gresham.

Eulogy
Allen Brooks Gresham
Allen Brooks Gresham of San Bernardino Lodge No. 178 was born on
May 10, 1931. He was initiated into El Centro Lodge No. 384, now Imperial Lodge
No. 390, on August 8th 1955, passed to the degree of Fellow Craft on November
22, 1955 and raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason on December 29th,
1955. He was Master of San Bernardino Lodge and Grand Master of Masons in
California. San Bernardino Lodge honored him with the Hiram Award in 1993. He
was a 33 degree Scottish Rite Mason and had been honored by several Masonic
Organizations. He laid down his working tools after 58 years of service to our
beloved fraternity and ascended to the celestial lodge above on April 20, 2014 at
the age of 83 years 11 months.
The Sacred Roll does not tell the tale of a man who touched so many
lives in his eighty three years of life; it just gives a hint of what he accomplished
in the fraternal world. Allen Brooks Gresham was much more than just his
Masonic honors.
Most Worshipful Gresham’s story begins during the great depression.
Allen was born in 1931 in the small town of Moorcroft, Wyoming (population
1009). He was the son of a schoolteacher from Missouri, who in those troubled
times had to travel from town to town, each year, seeking employment for the next
year. Those travels brought the Gresham family to El Centro, California, in the
Imperial Valley, where they were finally able to put down roots. No more traveling
for the Gresham family as his father’s teaching career prospered in El Centro with
him ultimately being selected as the Superintendent for the local school district.
It was in El Centro that Allen graduated from high school in 1949, the
same year that his father was Master of El Centro Lodge No. 384. In high school,
he was both an athlete and a scholar, which enabled him to be admitted to the
small, but prestigious, Occidental College in Los Angeles. He graduated with
a B.A. in 1953. Allen had served as Student Body President during his Senior
Year, but still found time to achieve sufficient academic honors to enable him to
enter Stanford Law School. While attending Stanford Law School in 1955, he
petitioned his father’s lodge, El Centro No. 384 and was initiated, passed and
raised before the end of 1955.
Allen graduated from Stanford Law School in 1956, at a time when
tensions were still high from the Korean War, when the military draft was after
almost every able-bodied young man. He joined the Army and spent the majority
of his service in Colorado dealing with top secret documents. Once he had
finished his Army enlistment, Allen returned to California, studied for and passed
the California Bar Exam, being admitted in June 1959.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

29

Allen began his law career with a small three-attorney office in San
Bernardino. Don Jordan, a Stanford Law School grad, and his partner John
Lonergan found Allen to be just what they were looking for in a young new
attorney and they immediately hired him on July 1, 1959. Thus began an amazing
44-year career in the practice of law.
Allen’s law practice dealt with civil litigation with a particular emphasis
in eminent domain, where he represented not only large corporations, but also
people whose property was being acquired for public purposes. Allen was an
extraordinarily bright and able trial attorney, but he always conducted himself as
a complete gentleman, never resorting to trickery or underhandedness. He had a
quick mind and a dry sense of humor that he enjoyed using at every opportunity.
His hard work and great skills paid off quickly. He was made a partner in the law
firm in 1962 just three years after being hired at the firm. He continued impressing
his new partners over the next eight years before being named the managing
partner in 1970. Over the next 33 years, Allen’s leadership took the firm from a
small four-person office to a firm of 55 attorneys with offices in San Bernardino,
Riverside, San Diego and Los Angeles.
When Allen found something great he knew that putting down roots
and making them grow was the best way to ensure a successful future. When he
met Clara Thompson, while they both attended Occidental College, he knew that
he had a found someone special and he wasn’t going to let her get away. They
were married in 1954 during his first year at Stanford Law. They formed a solid
partnership that lasted 60 years and produced two fine sons, Bruce and Brooks.
The family grew over the years to include five grandchildren. Allen and Clara
were members of the Presbyterian Church in San Bernardino and were active
in many of its activities including the Church’s Mariners Group. Clara shared
Allen’s commitment to public service and was an able partner in many of his
community and Masonic endeavors.
After Allen had put down business and family roots in San Bernardino,
he set about planting his Masonic roots there as well. In February of 1960, Allen
transferred his membership from his father’s lodge, El Centro Lodge No. 384, to
San Bernardino Lodge No. 178 where he was Master in 1967. He was an active
Past Master of his lodge and continued to be of service to his brethren. In May of
1993 the brethren of San Bernardino Lodge honored Allen with the Hiram Award.
When Allen started through the chairs to become Master, he began
working at the Grand Lodge level as well. In 1965 he was first appointed to the
Jurisprudence Committee, serving as Chairman in 1993 and again in 2008. He
served on the Trial Review Committee and on the Special Committee on Code
Revision, which between 1969 and 1973 rewrote the California Masonic Code. In
1972 he was selected by Most Worshipful William H. Price to serve as his Senior
Grand Deacon.

30

Proceedings of the

Allen was also very active in the concordant and appendant Masonic
Bodies. He was a member of the York Rite and Scottish Rite. He is a Past
Venerable Master of the San Bernardino Lodge of Perfection and was coroneted
a 33rd Degree Inspector General Honorary in 1991. He served as the Personal
Representative of the SGIG in the Valley of San Bernardino for many years. He
belonged to the Red Cross of Constantine, The Royal Order of Scotland, the
National Sojourners and High Twelve. He belonged to the Shrine and as a member
of Al Malaikah Temple he served for several years on the Board of Governors for
the Shrine Hospital for Children in Los Angeles, where he was recognized as
Board Member of the Year.
At the Annual Communication in 1993 he was elected Junior Grand
Warden and progressed through the elected progressive line of Grand Lodge
serving a term on all of the major Boards of Grand Lodge. He was elected
Grand Master of Masons in California in October of 1996. Following his service
as Grand Master he continued to serve Grand Lodge on committees including
Jurisprudence, and on the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California
where he served as President for three years.
As Grand Master, Most Worshipful Gresham chose the theme of “Quality
is the Key – You Can Make a Difference.” During his travels around the state as
Grand Master he encouraged the craft to look for ways to make their lodges and
their communities’ stronger better places. He got people talking about what could
be and should be done. He took time to spotlight local brothers who had made a
difference in other people’s lives. His efforts inspired many to make a difference.
He also emphasized the need for Masonic Unity of our Blue Lodges and of our
concordant and appendant bodies. He showed that working together we could
make our fraternity stronger and could achieve more of our goals. He was very
proud of the huge turnout for the Unity Day Ceremony held at the magnificent
Al Malaikah Shrine Auditorium. The 165-piece California Junior Philharmonic
Orchestra and the voices of Chapman College Chorus filled the auditorium
with beautiful music in support of the leadership of every concordant and
appendant body in California. It was a fitting tribute to Allen’s efforts to improve
Masonic Unity.
Allen’s theme, “Quality is the Key – You can make a Difference,” truly
reflects who he was. He believed that everyone has an obligation to use their
God-given talent to make the world a better place. He did not just give the idea
lip service, he lived it. At his law firm, he made it a requirement that every lawyer
to make a contribution in the community, either pro bono work or serving on
nonprofit boards. Allen led by example.
In San Bernardino he was active in Kiwanis. He served as the club
president and as Lieutenant Governor for the local region. Allen served on,
and was president of the local YMCA, and the local United Way. He strongly

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

31

supported the Inland Empire Symphony Association that brought quality music to
the Inland Empire community. He served as President of the Symphony Board in
1970/71 and again from 1989 to 1993.
He served as President of the San Bernardino County Bar Association in
1970. As he was retiring from the active practice of law in 2003 he received the
prestigious John B. Surr Award from the San Bernardino County Bar Association
for his outstanding career accomplishments as an attorney.
Allen served on the San Bernardino Valley College Board of Trustees.
His 35 years of service was the second longest service of any elected public college
trustee in the state of California. In recognition of his many years of service and
support of the College, the Board of Trustees named the art gallery on the San
Bernardino Valley College campus, in honor of Allen and Clara Gresham.
Allen was so grateful for the opportunities provided by his Occidental
College education that he served on the Occidental Board of Trustees for 23 years.
Due to Allen and Clara’s generosity and tireless support of their alma mater the
college named a dining hall for them.
Allen served as a member of the Mount San Jacinto Winter Park Authority.
It is the agency of the State of California that operates the Palm Springs Tram. He
served on the Board of the Saint Bernadine Medical Center in San Bernardino.
He was a City of San Bernardino booster and worked very hard with the Inland
Action, an influential business organization that promoted business activity in
San Bernardino.
There is no better tribute than the praise of those you have impacted by
your presence in their lives. Judith Valles, a two-term mayor of San Bernardino
said that “Allen was compassionate and everyone respected him who knew him.”
He was equally respected for his legal acumen and his devotion to his home
city. She used him as a sounding board when she was Mayor because he was
so knowledgeable and objective about any issue. Evelyn Wilcox, former mayor
of San Bernardino and a downtown business owner, said Allen was involved in
everything and shared everything he had. He gave freely of his time, talents and
treasure to make sure that his community was a better place than how he found
it. The lead in an obituary in one of his hometown papers summed up his service
to that community when it said, “A giant of San Bernardino civic life is gone.”
Allen was well known for saying that you should never join an
organization unless you were willing to serve as its President. He believed very
strongly that if you decided to be a part of an organization then you had to be
willing to work hard to see that it succeeded. If you were not willing to give it your
all then don’t get involved. Take your time, talent and treasure to an organization
that you could give your all to. Allen always gave his everything he could to every
organization he choose to joined and as a result he ended up presiding over nearly
everyone one of them.

32

Proceedings of the

Allen Brooks Gresham lived his life in keeping with the values of our
beloved fraternity and by his actions showed the world what masonic values mean
in everyday life. He made life better for countless others by his tireless efforts to
make his community a better place. He supported the arts, education, medicine
and numerous public works projects that helped make the Inland Empire a better
place for everyone to live. He lived a quality life and was the key to making a
difference in his community, our beloved fraternity and in the lives of all those he
inspired to help others. The world is a better place for his having been a part of it,
he truly made a difference, and he will be missed.
Soft and safe to thee, my brother, be thy resting place! Bright and glorious
be thy rising from it! Until then, dear brother, until then, farewell!

Election of Officers
The Grand Master then explained the balloting procedure for the election
of officers. No ballot would be necessary if the office was not contested. If more
than one nomination was received for an office, ballot cards would be distributed
for the purpose of balloting for that office.

seconded and carried that the nominations be closed, and that the Grand Secretary
be instructed to cast a unanimous ballot for Right Worshipful Russell E. Charvonia
to serve as Grand Master for the ensuing Grand Lodge year. Upon his acceptance,

Presentation of the Joe Jackson Award
This year, the Masonic Homes of California and our Grand Lodge were
pleased to present a new award in memory of our late Brother Joe Jackson.
Joe Jackson, a Mason for 60 years and Hiram Award recipient, served
Joseph L. Shell Daylight Lodge No. 837 and Heartland Lodge No. 576 for 17
years as secretary, assistant secretary, treasurer, and chaplain.
Joe exemplified Masonic relief and brotherly love. He reached out to
members and widows on a weekly basis, assisted with numerous applications to
MOS and the Masonic Homes, frequently called Masonic Assistance to check the
status of his member’s applications, and helped expedite the paperwork process.
He connected members and their families not only to Masonic services but also to
community resources and programs for veterans. If Joe Jackson was involved in
providing relief, the outcome was guaranteed to be a positive one!
Through his tireless efforts and determination to improve and grow
outreach, Joe was a catalyst for launching the successful Lodge Outreach strategic
initiative in Division IX. Joe passed away in 2012, leaving a legacy that set the
foundation for extending Masonic relief.
The Grand Master then asked everyone to join in welcoming Joe’s
widow, Mary Jackson, to the banquet this evening.
The Grand Master went on to explain that the Joe Jackson Lodge
Outreach Award is given to a lodge that has demonstrated excellence in outreach
to their members and widows. The first Joe Jackson Lodge Outreach Award
was presented to Consuelo Lodge No. 325 in Escondido for their extraordinary
outreach efforts this year.
The Grand Master then recognized the significant outreach contributions
La Mesa Lodge No. 407 made this year. They were instrumental in helping launch
the lodge outreach initiative in Division IX and developing training resources, and
they have developed an active and effective outreach program.
Grand Master Cooper then asked everyone to turn their attention to
a video presentation to learn more about the outreach program and all of the
programs of the Masonic Homes.
Following the video, those present enjoyed Masonic musical
performances by various members of the Craft as well as from students from the
San Francisco Conservatory of Music.
The Grand Master asked the Grand Chaplain to lead the benediction
after which the Grand Master invited all to attend the Public Ceremonies and
the Installation of Officers on Sunday morning, October 12, 2014 beginning
at 9:30 a.m.

Proceedings of the
Grand Master’s Youth Support Award

The Grand Master announced that four brothers had been selected to
receive the Grand Master’s Youth Support Award to recognize their outstanding
contribution to the Masonic youth orders. The Grand Master then called upon
Most Worshipful David R. Doan, Chairman of the Grand Lodge Youth Orders
Committee, to assist him in presenting the Grand Master’s Youth Support Award
to the following honorees:
Kenneth A. Gustafson
Brother Kenneth A. Gustafson is a Master Mason of Bay Cities Lodge
No. 337 in Richmond. His involvement with his lodge has included time as Tiler
and Building Manager.
Brother Gustafson’s true service to Masonry has been his long
involvement with the Masonic youth of Rainbow and DeMolay. Beginning
in the 1970’s, he has been a supporter and advisor for the San Pablo Rainbow
Assembly. He has been a member of the Advisory Council for over 25 years and
was the Chairman in 1998. In recognition of his service to the young ladies of the
assembly, he received the Grand Cross of Color.
Brother Ken’s work continued at the state level as well. He was
appointed State Rainbow Dad in 2005. He is a constant presence on the floor
at Grand Assembly and has devoted countless hours of his vacation time to the
Grand Assembly Office duplicating forms, preparing mailings, and performing
any other necessary tasks. Each year he travels to numerous events state-wide in
support of the girls of Rainbow.
Brother Gustafson’s commitment to youth extends to his professional
and community life as well. He served the County of Alameda as a juvenile
probation officer for over thirty years and volunteered his time at the San Leandro
Boys Club every Thursday evening. Following his retirement, he continued to
train and mentor new probation officers. He has spent his entire life as a mentor
and guide to future generations.
Brother Gustafson is seen as father figure by the members of Rainbow
and as a sterling example of Masonry by the parents and other adults working
beside him. He is a role model for Masons everywhere.
Philip Craig Harris
Brother Philip Craig Harris has been a devoted DeMolay since joining
Napa Chapter, Order of DeMolay at the age of 14. He has been a Master Mason
for over fifty years. He is the Treasurer of Napa Valley Lodge No. 93, a position
he has held for the past eleven years. Brother Harris is also the Chairman of the
Advisory Council for Napa Chapter, Order of DeMolay.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

49

After joining DeMolay, Brother Craig held several offices and moved
through the chairs to become Master Councilor of his chapter in 1957. He served
as the Master Councilor of the Redwood Empire Division and was appointed
State Junior Steward in 1959. Recognizing his leadership, his fellow DeMolays
elected him State Senior Councilor and State Master Councilor in succeeding
years. One of his fondest memories is of attending the first International Supreme
Council Session held in Vancouver, British Columbia—the first to be held outside
of the United States.
Brother Harris’ service to DeMolay continued as an adult volunteer in
the capacity of Dad Advisor of the Redwood Empire Division, District Deputy
for the jurisdiction of Northern California, and as the Chairman of the Advisory
Council for Napa Chapter. In recognition of his many years of dedication, the
Order of DeMolay has bestowed upon him many awards and honors including
Degree of Chevalier, the Cross of Honor, and the DeMolay Legion of Honor.
Brother Harris is an active member of Napa Valley Lodge No. 93. In
addition to his service as the lodge treasurer, he is the President of the St. Helena
Masonic Hall Association and has overseen the hall association’s renovation and
resurgence as a vibrant Masonic building. He was recognized by Napa Valley
Lodge No. 93 and Yount Lodge No. 12 as Mason of the Year in 2009 and he
received the Hiram Award in 2003.
Brother Craig Harris demonstrates the finest ideals of Masonry
and DeMolay.
Kendall R. Mills
Worshipful Brother Kendall R. Mills, a Past Master of Friendship Lodge
No. 210 in San Jose, has served Job’s Daughters since 2002 at both the local and
state level. Currently, he is the Associate Bethel Guardian of Bethel No. 129 in
San Jose and serves as the Grand Chaplain of the Grand Guardian Council.
Brother Mills has been a stalwart supporter of Bethel No. 129. In his
capacity as Associate Bethel Guardian, he assists the Bethel Guardian in the
performance of her duties working closely with the young ladies of the bethel.
He has performed his own duties with great distinction as he verifies the Masonic
relationships of every girl petitioning the bethel for membership and regularly
audits the bethel books. As the Grand Chaplain, Brother Mills travels throughout
the state visiting with members and bethels, inspiring their continued work and
success, and promoting the good of the order.
In addition to service to Job’s Daughters, Brother Mills has served as an
advisor for Campbell Chapter, Order of DeMolay, in San Jose, assisting the young
men of the chapter with learning and performing their ritual as well as with their
individual leadership development.

50

Proceedings of the

Brother Mills remains an active and dedicated Masonic leader. He has
served his lodge as an officer every year since 2002 including Master in 2008.
From 2009 to 2013, Brother Mills served as an inspector for the Grand Lodge of
California. He served on the Grand Lodge Fraternal Support Services Committee
for four years, three as chairman. He is now the chairman of the Public Schools
Advisory Council. Brother Kendall was recognized for his service to his lodge
and Freemasonry with the Hiram Award in 2010.
Robert Scott Shepard
Brother Robert Scott Shepard has been an active Mason of Old West
Lodge No. 813 and supporter of DeMolay for over thirty years.
Brother Shepard began his Masonic experience as a young man when he
joined Canoga Park Chapter, Order of DeMolay. As a youth leader, he served as
Master Councilor of his chapter.
As an adult leader, he has served Old West Chapter in several capacities
including Chapter Dad. In 2009, he assumed responsibility for Neo-Trital League
growing the league from two struggling chapters to eight active chapters-the
largest league in Southern California. Brother Scott efforts are credited as a major
factor in the resurgence of DeMolay in Southern California. He is presently an
Assistant to the Executive Officer for the jurisdiction and was elected a Deputy
Member of the International Supreme Council in 2011.
In recognition of his outstanding leadership and support of DeMolay,
Brother Shepard received the Degree of Chevalier, the Cross of Honor, and the
DeMolay Legion of Honor. He was the 2010 Advisor of the Year for Southern
California DeMolay and received the prestigious Guild of the Leathern Apron.
Brother Scott strives to integrate DeMolay into the Masonic family and
community identifying numerous opportunities for cooperation and service. He
sees that the DeMolay are regularly present at Masonic family events and is the
driving force behind a stronger relationship between the Masonic youth and the
Midnight Mission. His efforts teach the true meaning family and charity to our
youth. He continues to place the development and education of Masonic youth
above his own interests demonstrating the tenets of Masonry to future generations
of young men and women.
The Grand Master directed the Grand Marshal to escort the recipients

INSTALLATION OF GRAND LODGE OFFICERS

Officers were installed by Most Worshipful Larry L. Adamson, Past Grand
Master. He was assisted by Most Worshipful Harry L. Maynard, Honorary
Installing Officer, Most Worshipful John F. Lowe as Master of Ceremonies, and
Most Worshipful M. William Holsinger as Installing Chaplain. Grand Lodge was
raised by Mr. Keith and Miss Alissa Charvonia, son and daughter of the Grand
Master-elect.

Grand Master’s Message
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State
of California:
Past Grand Masters, Past Grand Officers, Grand Officers, Worshipful
Masters, my brethren all.
Welcome to the 165th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
California, here in the City and County of San Francisco.
Section 404.130 of the California Masonic Code requires the
Grand Master to “Present, at each Annual Communication, a written message
setting forth:
•
•
•

All his official acts during the year.
The general condition of Masonry within this Jurisdiction; and
Recommending such legislation as he deems necessary or expedient for
the welfare of the craft.

Lodges with Problems:
When Grand Lodge grants a charter to a Masonic lodge there is the
expectation that it will govern itself in accordance with the Ancient Landmarks
of Freemasonry, and more specifically, in accordance with the provisions of the
California Masonic Code. There is also the expectation that a Masonic lodge
will be able to confer the three degrees of Ancient Craft Masonry in accordance
with the approved Ritual of our jurisdiction. If a lodge is unable to fulfill these
expectations to the satisfaction of the Grand Master, the charter of the lodge can
be suspended. The suspension of a charter is intended to give a lodge time to
reorganize itself and remedy what is wrong. At the beginning of my term as Grand
Master I extended the suspension of the following four lodges:
•
•
•
•

Sublime-Benicia Lodge No. 5, at Benicia;
Santa Lucia Lodge No. 302, at King City;
Foothill Lodge No. 305, at Monrovia; and
Vallee de France Lodge No. 329, at North Hollywood

I was able to return the charter of Santa Lucia Lodge No. 302 in January,
2014, and the charter of Vallee de France Lodge No. 329 in September, 2014. The
situation at Sublime-Benicia Lodge No. 5 will be explained in connection with
Grand Master’s Recommendation No. 5. Foothill Lodge No. 305 has not been
successful in resolving the issues at that lodge, and still suffers from a lack of
officers, administrative problems, and the inability to confer the degrees.

58

Proceedings of the

Unfortunately I had to add to the list of suspended lodges two more.
In January I suspended the charter of North Hollywood Lodge No. 542 for
defying my edict that they not sell their building until they had complied with the
requirements of the California Masonic Code. Then, in May, 2014, I suspended
the charter of Three Great Lights Lodge No. 651 at Menlo Park for failure to
sustain qualified officers for the lodge, and failure to be able to confer the degrees
of Masonry. In each case, much needs to be done for these two lodges to be able
to return to a self-governing status as a regular lodge in this jurisdiction.
Showcasing Freemasonry:
The suspension of the charters of lodges is a negative for Freemasonry
in this jurisdiction, but fortunately we also had examples of showcasing
Freemasonry at its best. This year we had a number of events designed to let
our local communities know more about Freemasonry. Among them were
the following:
•

“There Was a Seafaring Man”: In November, 2013, we celebrated
Freemasonry in the Pacific in conjunction with the Maritime Museum
of San Diego. In addition to commemorating the 100th anniversary of
Coronado Lodge No. 441 and Amity Lodge No. 442, we told the story
of the founding of one of the most famous lodges in Hawaii – Lodge “Le
Progrès de l’Océanie,” a lodge that once was under the jurisdiction of the
Grand Lodge of California.

•

“Freemasonry in the Gold Rush Country”: In June we celebrated our
Masonic roots in the Gold Rush Country of California. Two events were
worthy of note here:
•

Rededication of Masonic Hall and Museum at Columbia
Historic State Park: In 1949 the Grand Lodge of California
erected a replica Masonic hall at Columbia. This building
included a lodge room on the top floor, and a museum on the
ground floor. Thanks to a generous donation from the California
Masonic Foundation, we were able to completely renew the
interior of the building, and create a contemporary exhibit to
tell the story of Freemasonry during Gold Rush times. This
magnificent project was a combined effort of many, but the
main credit must go to our Grand Secretary, Very Worshipful
Brother Allan L. Casalou, who conceived of the project, and
carried it to its impressive conclusion. We now have a museum
worthy of California Freemasonry, one that will be visited by
thousands each year, who will learn about our important role in
the creation of the State of California.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California
•

59

Re-Enactment of the 1861 Cornerstone Laying Ceremony
at the California State Capitol: A week later Grand Lodge
assembled in Sacramento and re-enacted the 1861 cornerstone
laying ceremony for the California State Capitol. Conducted on
the impressive grounds of our State Capitol, the Grand Lodge
Officers were led in by more than 250 Masons, each one clad
in his white lambskin apron. Credit for the organization of
this event goes to the planning committee which worked for
three years to make it the success that it was. And credit for
leading this planning committee goes to Worshipful Brother
Phil Hardiman, who spent many hours of hard work with eager
and dedicated volunteers to make it happen.

On the World Stage:
I was privileged to serve as Chairman of the Conference of Grand Masters
of Masons in North America in Baltimore, Maryland, last February. California
brought to the conference a presentation on “Civility and Freemasonry,” and from
this beginning came the “Masonic Civility Project of North America.” Credit must
be given to our Deputy Grand Master, Right Worshipful Bro. Russell Charvonia,
who conceived the idea, and helped bring it to the attention of the grand lodges of
Canada and the United States. You will hear more about this project in the very
near future.
In May I led a delegation of California Masons to the World Conference
of Regular Grand Lodges in Bucharest, Romania. I was asked to conduct one of
six workshops for the conference, and shared the platform with the Grand Master
of the Grand Lodge of the State of Israel. Our subject was: How the Ancient
Principles and Experiences of Freemasonry Can Contribute to the Making of a
Better World.” It was inspiring to share this with the Grand Masters, and other
leaders, of almost a hundred grand lodges from every continent in the world. As
you may know, the next World Conference will be held in our Memorial Temple
right here in San Francisco in November, 2015. I was asked to represent North
American Freemasonry as a member of the new Advisory Committee for the
conference – one of seventeen Masons from around the world who was asked
to serve.
On our way to Bucharest we had an opportunity to visit Austria, and to
meet Freemasons in the home of Mozart and Haydn. Our delegation attended an
Entered Apprentice Degree close to the place where these two famous composers
were made Masons in the 18th century, and I had the pleasure of sitting in the East
with the Grand Master of Austria. After the conference in Bucharest, the Grand
Secretary and I attended a series of meetings in Paris, France, gaining information
to assist our Grand Lodge in understanding the complex and evolving Masonic
situation in that country.

60

Proceedings of the

Attending the World Conference brought to mind a problem which I
believe that Freemasonry must address in the very near future, and which should
afford our Grand Lodge an opportunity to take the lead. Freemasonry around
the world is still divided by issues that are difficult to solve, but which merit our
attention. Closer to home, I have a concern for which a solution must be found.
Our Grand Lodge is very proud of the close relationship which we have with
the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California. We are in amity not only with that
Grand Lodge, but with many other Prince Hall grand lodges in the United States.
However, there remain a few states which have not yet worked out a relationship
between the original grand lodge in that state, and the Prince Hall grand lodge
in that jurisdiction. As a result, California Masons can sit with a Prince Hall
Mason from those jurisdictions while in a Prince Hall lodge in California, but
cannot invite that brother to his own lodge – a lodge under the jurisdiction of the
Grand Lodge of California. I believe that the time has come to seek a remedy
for this situation. It is therefore my recommendation that our incoming Grand
Master consider assembling a blue ribbon task force to address the issues of
recognition with other grand lodges, not only with the Prince Hall grand lodges
in American states where we cannot at present recognize these grand lodges, but
issues of recognition in France and in other parts of the world. California has the
opportunity to lead in this important area, and if the best minds that we can secure
work on solutions that are consistent with the principles of Freemasonry, I believe
that we can take the high road of brotherhood in helping the Masonic world at
large find a new way to reach out to our “separated brethren” who “must else have
remained at a perpetual distance.”
The World of Academia and Freemasonry:
Our Grand Lodge has sponsored three academic conferences this year.
The first of these was in November, 2013, at the San Francisco Scottish Rite.
Partnering with the Policy Studies Organization in Washington, DC, we presented
four lecturers on two prominent California Masons. The first was Thomas Starr
King, a member of Oriental Lodge No. 144 (now Phoenix Lodge No. 144) and our
Grand Orator in 1863. The second was Earl Warren, who was our Grand Master
in 1936. Grand Master Warren went on to become Governor of California, and
the Chief Justice of the United States Supreme Court. Both of these outstanding
Masons had a significant impact on our country, and the conference was an
opportunity to understand each of the better. A highlight of the conference was the
joint laying of a wreath at the tomb of Thomas Starr King with the Grand Master
of the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California.
In April we sponsored the Third International Conference on
Freemasonry at the University of California, Los Angeles. Again, top scholars
participated in this academic event, demonstrating the importance of the study
of Freemasonry in the world of academia. Finally, we presented the Fourteenth

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

61

Annual California Masonic Symposium in both Northern California and Southern
California. This year the topic was “The Creation of the American Republic,”
and the lectures concerned the importance of Freemasonry and its ideals in
the evolution of our American system of government. Your Grand Master was
honored by being created a Fellow of the Institute for Masonic Studies, which
sponsors the symposium each year.
The Proceedings will list the events which I attended as Grand Master,
and I will not attempt here to list them all. My Decisions and Recommendations
will be presented separately when we consider the legislation later in this session.
This brings me to the conclusion of my message as Grand Master, and in closing
I would share with you some personal observations, and express some personal
appreciations to those who have helped make this year a successful one for our
Grand Lodge.
In 2005 the Grand Lodge Officers Jewels were stolen. The burglary
occurred while the Grand Lodge Office was under construction, and the new
security system had not yet been installed. The jewels were covered by our Grand
Lodge insurance, but when the insurance money was received, it was used to
replace our Grand Lodge aprons and collars that are used at our public ceremonies,
such as cornerstones. That was a wise use of the funds at the time because that
affected our public image as a Grand Lodge. Nevertheless, I was constantly
reminded each year by the empty jewel case at the Annual Communication that
we had not replaced the jewels. Last year, thanks to hard work by our Immediate
Past Grand Master, Most Worshipful John Lowe, we were able to finally replace
the jewels. It took all this year to make them, and the Grand Lodge Officers are
now proudly wearing them. My thanks go to Most Worshipful Bro. John for his
commitment to this project, and to our Grand Secretary who worked with the
artist who had made the original jewels in the 1990’s to make new ones. It is a
fitting close to this issue which began while I was your Grand Secretary, and am
now able to report it to you as your Grand Master.
This year I chose as my theme “Freemasonry – Our Moral Compass.”
It was intended to remind us that the principles of Freemasonry must be more
than antiquarian curiosities which we have inherited from ages past. They are
living principles which can and should guide our every action. We are reminded
of that each time that a lodge is closed when the Chaplain asks that God may grant
us the wisdom and strength to “carry out of the lodge those great moral duties
which are inculcated in it.” In my travels this year I have had an opportunity to
share that commitment with others, not only in California, but around the world. I
was privileged to lead one of the workshops at the World Conference of Regular
Grand Lodges in Romania last May, and the theme of that workshop was “How
the Ancient Principles of Freemasonry Can Make a Better World.” I was joined
as a co-presenter in this workshop with the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of
the State of Israel, Most Worshipful Bro. Albert-Avi Baranes. Together we shared

62

Proceedings of the

a vision of Freemasonry that can, if truly believed and truly practiced, bring
peace to our troubled world, and make the ancient principles by which we live as
Masons the wellspring of brotherhood for all humanity.
Finally, I want to thank all those who made this year a success. It is a
truism that no one can accomplish anything alone, but this year was a salient
reminder of that fact. It would take far too long to personally mention all those
who should be mentioned. However, I will pay special tribute to the following:
•
•
•
•
•

•

To our Grand Lecturer, Very Worshipful Bro. Jack Rose, whose vision of
how Freemasonry is expressed through our Ritual has been an inspiration
to me, and to many others;
To our Grand Secretary, Very Worshipful Bro. Allan Casalou, whose
advice and counsel I have constantly sought, and whose staff worked
tirelessly to make this year a success.
To our Grand Treasurer, Very Worshipful Bro. Ray Schmaltz, who
contributed so much to our deliberations;
To our Senior and Junior Grand Wardens, Right Worshipful Bro. Dave
Perry and Right Worshipful Bro. John Heisner, who formed an invaluable
part of our Executive Team;
To our Deputy Grand Master, Right Worshipful Bro. Russell Charvonia,
I could not have had greater support this year that his. Due to health
issues I was unable at the last moment to handle certain Grand Lodge
events, including two cornerstone ceremonies. Russ not only handled
them with ease, but did so graciously even when he had little notice that
he would have to open Grand Lodge and take care of everything. His
leadership of our Grand Lodge goes back a long way, and the year that
is almost past has demonstrated more than anything else how valued his
talents are. Thank you, Bro. Russ, for your friendship and support on
many, many occasions!
Finally, to my wife, Heather. Without her constant support over the years
that I was Grand Secretary I could not have served Grand Lodge for the
eighteen years that I held that position. And then her continued support
through the years as Junior Grand Warden, Senior Grand Warden,
Deputy Grand Master, and finally Grand Master, has been beyond the
expectation that any man should have. Although she is not in this room
today to hear it, Heather I love you, and I am so grateful that you have
been by my side all the way!

When I was installed last October 6, I closed my remarks with a poem
called “Anyway”. It has been a guide for me all this year, and with this poem I
will close these remarks:

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

63

“Anyway”
People are often unreasonable, illogical, and self-centered;
Forgive them anyway.
If you are kind, people may accuse you of selfish, ulterior motives;
Be kind anyway.
If you are successful, you will win some false friends and some true enemies;
Succeed anyway.
If you are honest and frank, people may cheat you;
Be honest and frank anyway.
What you spend years building, someone could destroy overnight;
Build anyway.
If you find serenity and happiness, they may be jealous;
Be happy anyway.
The good you do today, people will often forget tomorrow;
Do good anyway.
Give the world the best you have, and it may never be enough;
Give the world the best you’ve got anyway.
You see, in the final analysis, it is between you and your God;
It was never between you and them anyway.
Respectfully submitted,
John L. Cooper III, Grand Master

Report of the Deputy Grand Master
2014/2015 Grand Lodge Budget
Russell E. Charvonia, Deputy Grand Master
As your Deputy Grand Master, it is my duty to prepare and present
to you a budget for the upcoming fiscal year. I am grateful for the support of
the brethren who adopted the per capita proposal I submitted at the 2013
Annual Communication.
Since that time, I have refined the budget while monitoring current
income and expenses as well as our membership activity. Earlier this year, I had
the opportunity to discuss the budget with our Masters and Wardens at the various
retreats. Their input over the last two years has been very helpful to me. I have
also worked with the Grand Lodge Finance and Insurance Committees, our Grand
Treasurer, Grand Secretary and our incredible finance staff to be sure that we
are operating in an efficient and prudent manner. As a result of this teamwork,
I now place the attached budget before you for consideration at the upcoming
Annual Communication.
Two years ago, the delegates of the Grand Lodge adopted Resolution
11‐07, which required Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons to pay dues
and to be included on the membership rolls. As such, the Per Capita is now based
on the total number of Masons on the rolls, not just Master Masons. While our
membership projections have been very predictable over the last decade, it was
very difficult to accurately project just how many of our Entered Apprentice and
Fellow Craft Masons would stay on the rolls versus being suspended for non‐
payment of dues.
I am pleased to inform you that the assumptions we used when I
requested of you a Per Capita rate of $36.50 turned out to be fairly accurate.
We had originally built the budget on 52,632 paid memberships, and the actual
number came in at 52,269.
Total Income for the next fiscal year is estimated to be $2,792,847. The
income includes:
•

Per Capita revenue of $1,907,819 representing 68.3% of the total income.

•

The dividend from the Nob Hill Masonic Center, which will be $265,000
or 9.5% of the total income.

•

The grant from the California Masonic Foundation of $130,000 for
Masonic education and leadership training, representing 4.7% of
total income.

84

Proceedings of the
•

A distribution from investments of $159,727, representing 5.7% of
total income.

•

Revenue from application fees from all lodges and dues from the Grand
Master’s Lodge totaling $65,525 or 2.4% of the total income.

•

Other revenue from reimbursements from investments and Masonic
Service Bureaus of $230,299, representing 8.2% of total income.

There also is a one‐time source of income in the proposed budget which
you approved last year wherein you reserved $34,478 of the Fiscal Year 2014
surplus to be used in Fiscal Year 2015, representing 1.2% of total income.
Expenses exclusive of depreciation for the next fiscal year are estimated
to be $2,775,423. These expenses are divided between fraternal, appropriations
and general and administrative. In many areas, we have kept expenses at the same
level as the current year. The following represent the changes in expenses.
•

I have included $5,000 for minor expenses associated with my objective
of our doing local community service projects.

•

I have increased our support for youth orders, as I believe we need to put
our money and efforts behind our verbal support for our youth.

•

Lodge insurance will increase by 2.6%.

•

Total Personal Costs‐Increased 14.1%

•

◦◦

Wages will increase by approximately 3.0% representing 2.1% of
our total Personnel cost increase.

◦◦

A new Intacct position, representing a 3.9% of the total Personnel
cost increase, was added to support our work in training, State and
Federal tax return preparation for all lodges, our work reinstating
lost tax exemptions and other tax related issues.

◦◦

Other employment related expenses, driven particularly by health
insurance premiums, represented 8.1% of our total Personnel
Cost increase.

Items subject to inflation are planned to increase by 2%‐3%.

The projected net revenue after expenses is approximately $5,000. As you can
see, this is a razor‐thin margin. We will need to monitor our income and expenses
very carefully to make this budget works.
There has been a lot of thought and consideration given to this budget. I sincerely
appreciate the contributions by many different brethren. With the adoption of this
budget, we will be able to maintain the programs and services we now provide to
our lodges and members and we will make an important investment in the future.
I thank you, again, for your previous support and ask for your support now as we
consider this budget for our coming fiscal year.

GRAND LODGE OF FREE AND ACCEPTED

Fiscal Year 2014/2015
Russ Charvonia, Deputy Grand Master
Revenue Analysis

The Grand Lodge has several sources of income. Historically, the primary revenue source has been
per capita and degree fees. The Grand Lodge Endowment Fund was created in 1992 and generates
investment income. To better manage those monies, a four and a half-percent spending policy has
been instituted, calculated on a rolling five-year valuation to ensure the preservation of the fund
principle. The Grand Lodge may have other income like interest on bank accounts and other
financial instruments from time to time. In 2004, the California Masonic Foundation included in its
mission the funding of Masonic education and leadership training programs and now provides a grant
for those purposes. In 2005, the delegates of the 156th Annual Communication adopted a $30
application fee to be paid to Grand Lodge by all applicants for degrees and out-of-state affiliations.
The Grand Lodge manages different service bureaus throughout the state and receives
reimbursement for those expenses. The Grand Lodge also manages the investments of its related
entities and receives reimbursement equal to the cost of those services. The Grand Lodge is the sole
shareholder of the Nob Hill Masonic Center Inc., and may receive dividends on the profits of the
corporation.
