Installation Address

Russell E. Charvonia
Grand Master of Masons in California, 2014-2015
Brethren, Ladies, and Friends;
I stand before you for the first time as your Grand Master, very humbled,
and with tremendous pride. Freemasonry provides the opportunity for ordinary
men to do extraordinary things. And while this is not a position I sought, it is
one that I will serve to the best of my ability, and with a fervency and zeal for
our beloved Institution. My love for our fraternity is second only to my love and
appreciation of my family.
And it is with the help of an incredible team of Grand Lodge officers
and their families that we intend to roll up our shirtsleeves, not only to move the
fraternity of Freemasonry forward, but to also work hard to repair our world.
Some folks have told me that they are troubled by the notion that our
world is in need of repair; that I am implying that the world about us is somehow
broken. No, my friends, I am not implying any such thing. I am stating, without
equivocation that our society is in desperate need of repair. I further believe that it
is incumbent upon us, as Masons, using the tools and implements, the language,
and primarily the tenets and values that we hold so dear and constantly strive to
internalize, to do all that we can to repair this world.
So how will we bring about such monumental reformation? Those who
belong to service groups such as Rotary and Kiwanis know that they are repairing
the world through their acts, by their deeds. They are certainly accomplishing
much and are indeed making our world a better place. As Masons, however, we
take a more systemic, intrinsic approach. We are convinced that when we work to
improve ourselves, we are able to make even more enduring enhancements to our
society as we move through the various circles of our lives.
Our Masonic teachings lead us to such personal growth. It is up to each
of us to continue to progress. We do this by realizing that each of us is an imperfect
ashlar, with many rough and superfluous edges that need to be constantly chipped
away and honed, and that we need to always be vigilant to continue that work.
We talk much about the universality of Freemasonry, and how it
celebrates the brotherhood of man, under the fatherhood of God. And yet I often
wonder whether we are doing all we can to not only accept, but also to appreciate
our differences as friends and brothers. To advance this cause, we recently formed
a task force under the guidance of Most Worshipful Cooper to help us understand
the different cultures within California Masonry. It is my hope that by facilitating
open and honest conversations, we will gain an understanding that will enable us
to show the rest of the world how we can find accord among diverse cultures and
opinions, while allowing each of us to experience the personal growth we all seek.

94

Proceedings of the

As we go about repairing our world, I challenge each of us to demonstrate
that brotherly love, care and compassion that is so much a part of who we are
as Masons.
So as we pursue our respective journeys over the course of this year, I
ask that you join me in focusing on bridging our cultural and religious differences.
And as each of us grows in our acceptance and appreciation of others, we will
then allow the ripples to spread across the spheres of our own lives.
I had occasion last year to meet a Past Grand Chaplain from the
Grand Lodge of Israel. This brother shared with me how incredible it is that in
his homeland, Muslims, Jews and Christians are able to sit together in perfect
harmony, as friends and brothers, during their lodge meetings. If Masons can
lay aside their considerable differences for 90 minutes at a time, shouldn’t we be
able to find ways to expand this harmony outside our lodges and into our greater
communities? I believe we can do just that. And I believe it is imperative that we
do so, now, before it is too late.
We will have a chance to witness this harmonic convergence first hand
when we make our way to the Holy Land this coming May. This will truly be
a life-changing trip. In addition to learning about and admiring our Masonic
heritage, we will focus on gaining a better understanding of the three Abrahamic
religions. It is my hope that we will each leave Israel with a greater understanding
and appreciation of those religions other than our own.
Come along with Linda and me as we walk in the steps of Solomon and
Hiram, and experience the very foundations of Masonry. We will join with our
brethren from the Middle East and experience a special brand of Freemasonry.
We will see the sun rise over the Sea of Galilee and toil in Solomon’s quarries.
We will even visit a chocolate factory. Please plan to join us on this journey back
in time to Masonry’s origins and to see where our gentle Craft might lead us in
the future.
Here at home, I am very excited that we will be scheduling Brotherhood
Degree Exemplifications across the state. In these ceremonies, brethren of
different cultures will exemplify either the Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft
degree, each working in their own language. I envision these to be a lot of fun
and educational for both the participants and sideliners. Hopefully the foods of
each of the cultures will also be featured, because we all know that we Masons
excel at eating. While these will not be actual conferrals of degrees, I believe they
will demonstrate for us, in living color, the true universality of Masonry. Your
Assistant Grand Lecturers will be imparting more information on these as the
year progresses.
As we grow personally, and become more understanding and accepting
of those who are different from ourselves, we can really get to work repairing
the world around us. I believe one of the greatest contributions we can make to
society is to share our Masonic ideals in an effort to create a more civil world. At

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

95

almost every turn in our daily lives, we encounter a sickening level of incivility.
We see it on our roadways, within our families, our workplaces, government, and
even, my brethren, within the confines of our lodges.
And yet we seem willing to tolerate this sorry state of affairs. Perhaps our
indifference stems from a sense of helplessness or not understanding how we can
turn the tide; or that we feel that we lack the power as a single person to change
things. Maybe there are some who actually benefit from rampant incivility.
Well I believe that as Masons, we have an absolute duty to do what we
can to address this social plight. Think about it; don’t we have the tools, the
language, and most importantly the values and tenets to help those around us treat
each other with dignity and respect? Don’t we have the power to create a legacy
of lasting good in society?
Last February a group of brethren from across North America began
working toward building such a legacy. This group has two primary objectives
at this point:
The first is to create a toolbox that will help us to be more civil in our
own lives; with our families, lodges, workplaces and greater communities. It is
our vision that this “symbolic toolbox” will be made available to every one of
the nearly two million Masons across North America. Given the proper tools and
skills, mighty cathedrals were built by the operative Masons of old. What sort of
interpersonal edifices might we, as speculative Masons, create for today’s society
when we hold the proper tools?
We are also looking for ways that, as Masons, we can bring together other
organizations and associations who are attempting to restore civility to society. It
is well known that Masons have long served as bridge builders for groups of
disparate thought and opinion. I think we can serve as catalysts to help these
groups to gain greater effectiveness, to provide the momentum and cohesiveness
that will allow civility to be nurtured in all walks of life.
My brothers and friends, if we don’t step up, today, to correct the
situation, who will? And if we allow this rampant incivility to continue, what kind
of world will be leaving for our children, and for our children’s children?
I ask that you join me on this journey to create a more civil society. We
can each start by examining our own daily behavior, and look for ways to improve
how we treat those in our lives. We can create greater civility in the most common
of our activities, say our own driving, for instance. And we can work to subdue
our passions and channel our desires for greater good. What would happen, for
example, if we found a way to grant the benefit of the doubt to others in our midst?
Imagine how much stress could be relieved by our simply assuming that most
people around us are decent, well-intended folks, even if they hold opinions or
attitudes that differ from our own?

96

Proceedings of the

And through the language and working tools of Masonry, we can then
teach others how to engage in difficult conversations. Picture the good that can
come from those around us learning how to engage in constructive and civil
dialogue, as opposed to name calling and finger wagging.
And then, using the toolkit we are creating, we can repair our world by
helping others to be more civil. By practicing out of our lodges the lessons we are
learning within it, I have every confidence that, together, we can turn this tide and
help to create a more civil society.
My brothers, the world is ready for what we have to offer. And Masonry
stands ready to come to its aid. While we don’t own this civility effort, we can
serve a vital role.
I have shared many ways that we can personally grow in order to
repair our world. And I said earlier that other service groups such as Rotary
and Kiwanis do many good acts. I think it is also critical that we, as members of
the entire Masonic family, get out into our local communities and find ways to
make improvements, either for strength or ornament. I have occasion to talk with
many of our newer brethren about their Masonic journey, and when I hear any
disappointment in the Masonic experience from these newer, younger members,
it is generally that they expected we would be more active with our communities.
And they are right—we do need to do more than just work to improve ourselves.
We can be more overt in our civic efforts and become a more vital link for
our communities.
Based on those expressions, our Grand Lodge officers and families will
focus this year on working with our local lodge brethren, our youth orders and
concordant Masonic organizations to roll up our shirtsleeves and get our hands
dirty in doing local service projects. I want to identify our older lodge brothers
and widows who need things done around their homes. Let’s find schools, parks
and beaches that need beautification. And we can even work on our own lodge
buildings. Can you imagine the message we will send to our Masonic family and
greater communities when we have 100 or more people performing hundreds of
hours of labor in a single afternoon? I think we can repair our world in very
tangible ways. And the truth is, we all feel better about ourselves when we do
things for others.
You might be able to hear my passion when I say that I believe in our
ability to repair our world. I am also convinced that in order to make a lasting
difference, we need to start by investing in our own youth. If you harbored any
doubt of the qualities and capabilities of our youth, I am sure those reservations
are have been doused after what we heard this morning. My brethren, we often
say that this next generation of young people is our future. If this is true (and it
seems logical enough to me), then it is imperative that we are part of their present.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

97

This consists of more than simply providing support at the organizational
level. It means being there every step of the way, to provide the necessary support
and provide guidance so our young people can learn from our example. It means
getting to know them as individuals and letting them be a part of our lives. It
means accepting roles as their advisors and chaperones and providing financial
support. It also means keeping them safe and giving them opportunities.
We all know our young people learn by observing our actions, not by
hearing what we tell them. Please join me in letting them see us in our lodges
and halls, and at their chapters, bethels and assemblies. I challenge each Mason
to attend a Youth Order function this year. Arrive early and stay late. I promise
you will be inspired and amazed by the experience, and it will mean the world
to the kids.
I am grateful to Worshipful Brother Glenn Woody for agreeing to serve as
the chairman of our Youth Orders committee for this year. Glenn will be reaching
out to the leaders of our lodges to share ways in which you can work along side
our youth, for the betterment of our entire Masonic family. The committee has
been working in preparation for the coming year on some very exciting projects,
with the help and contributions of the adult leaders of our Masonic Youth Orders.
One of the things you can do to support our youth orders is to go to
Masons4Youth.org, right now. Well you may want to wait until we are finished
here and then go check it out. Each of us can step up and get certified as an adult
volunteer for one or more of our Masonic youth groups. We are not yet to the
point where we have too many adult volunteers!
And then I hope you will join us at the first of what will become an
annual Harvest Festival at our Union City Masonic Home on Saturday, November
15th. At that time, we will have the extreme pleasure of re-dedicating DeMolay
Drive, which leads the way to our magnificent facility.
This is a terrific opportunity to bridge the generations of our Masonic
Home residents and our young people. And don’t worry, we will be looking to
dedicate Rainbow Way and Job’s Daughters Lane at the Home in the near future.
As California Masons, we have a long history of working to keep our
youngsters safe. One of the primary ways we have done this over the past 15-plus
years is through our KIDS Child ID program. Thousands of us have fingerprinted
and photographed hundreds of thousands of children over the years, at all sorts of
community events and schools.
And while we have made a big difference with this program, the truth
is that our local law enforcement agencies routinely provide this service, often
doing a better job than our system does. And yet, we all recognize the importance
of keeping our children safe and to be an integral part of our local communities.

98

Proceedings of the

I am therefore, introducing today, the In Case of Emergency, or ICE
Pack. As you can see on the screen, this bright orange envelope has important
instructions as to what to do in an automobile emergency, such as a wreck, tire
blowout or breakdown. The instructions are in big print, that can be read through
the tears of a frightened driver. And it includes helpful information that will come
in handy in time of panic.
This ICE Pack was developed by then 18-year old, Christian Wheeler,
who is now our brother from Washington Lodge No. 20 in Sacramento.
I believe the ICE Pack will allow us to help keep young drivers safe,
allow the opportunity for our lodge brethren to serve their communities, and
demonstrate to the world that Masonry is relevant and is making a difference, on
their behalf. The ICE Packs will feature and promote our youth orders, and since
they are designed with the young driver in mind, it is a good method to connect
with prospective members for our three youth groups, as well as potentially
interesting their parents in learning more about the family of Freemasonry.
You will each receive one of these kits as you exit today, and then each
lodge will be sent an initial shipment of 50 ICE Packs within the next few weeks.
Additional kits may be purchased at a cost of roughly $1 apiece. It is my hope
that you will distribute these at community and school events, either instead
of or in conjunction with the KIDS ID program. Please look for opportunities
where you can use this as a vehicle to give back to your community and help our
young people.
Thank you, Brother Christian for doing your part to repair our world.
As Masons, we have a proud history of helping our schools and students.
Over the past three years, we raised an incredible $1.2 million for the very
worthwhile Raising a Reader program. This will help some 50,000 of our children
learn to appreciate the world of reading over the next five years.
This year, we will focus our attention on keeping our children firesafe. We will work hard to save children from the life-changing horrors of burns
by bringing burn prevention education to “each child, each year” in California
schools. We will do this by supporting the Firefighters in Safety Education (FISE)
program, which is operated by the Alisa Ann Ruch Burn Foundation. This group
is responsible for the “Stop, Drop and Roll” effort that has saved enumerable
lives over the decades. This program will allow us to bring free burn prevention
education and materials to thousands of elementary school students every year.
Let me show you why this is so critical:
Linda and I have had the opportunity to experience Champ Camp on our
own. And an incredible experience it was. For one week, children between the
ages of 5 and 16 come together at Wonder Valley Camp outside of Fresno to be
kids; to have fun.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

99

However, the way I see it, our job is to put the camp out of business; to
see to it that there is no longer a need for burn survivors to have such a refuge for
a week, because our children are kept safe from such accidents.
To share with you why this is so important, I introduce to you author and
Brother Dan Caro.
Before you are a number of men and women who protect our lives and
property. These are our heroes. And Brother Dan, you are indeed a hero, for
providing inspiration and hope where others might have despaired.
Yesterday marked the conclusion of Fire Prevention Week. Accordingly,
I find it most appropriate that today we kick off this effort to keep our young
people fire safe throughout California.
This effort provides an opportunity for us to work closely with each of
our youth orders, Shrine Masons and the other members of the Masonic family to
make a profound difference in our communities as we aim to reach some 70,000
students every year for three years; students in your local schools. Because, my
friends, “Burns are Everyone’s Battle.”
We have just opened an online store called the Repair Shop, where you
can go buy really cool stuff, with all of the net proceeds going directly to support
our Firefighters in Safety Education effort.
We are facilitating this training in our schools because no child, or
parent, should ever have to come to grips with such horror. Accidental burns can
be prevented; and we know that a handful of simple and easily communicated
steps can save a life. It only takes a few seconds for an entire life to change! This
is where our partnership with the Burn Foundation comes in and why it is so vital.
There is a well-established principle in Freemasonry that in order to
maintain the sanctity of a Masonic lodge, neither religion nor partisan politics
are to be discussed within it. Well, my brethren, there are actually a total of four
taboo topics which are not to be brought into the lodge. The other two, you ask?
Well we cannot discuss traffic woes. You see, in our travels across this great state,
the Northerners are quite convinced that SoCal has the worst traffic in the world,
while when in the South, well the traffic up here is the nastiest. So in the name of
civility, we simply don’t raise this subject.
The other subject that is strictly verboten inside the lodge room,
especially at this time of year is, of course, baseball.
Because there is simply no bridge strong enough to get Giants and
Dodger fans to meet in the middle. But this cardinal rule is about to be broken,
because starting next season, Masons 4 Mitts will be expanded to include the LA
Dodgers Reviving Baseball in Inner Cities (RBI) program. This season here in
the north, we were able to donate more than 4,500 high quality baseball mitts to

100

Proceedings of the

underprivileged kids through the San Francisco Junior Giants Foundation. Next
year, we are looking to put some 10,000 mitts in the hands of deserving children
across the entire state.
We may need to suspend our civility efforts for a period, but I promise to
do all I can to temper my passions.
This is yet one more way we are able to demonstrate to our communities
that we care. This important and fun program goes a long way to helping to elevate
the image of our Craft in the eyes of the public.
As you can see we have very ambitious goals for our Fraternity. But
I have every confidence that California Masons are up to the task. And more
importantly, that the world is in dire need of what we have to offer.
My brethren, I believe the best days of Freemasonry are ahead of us,
not behind us. The teachings and principles of our gentle Craft are as important
and relevant to society today as they have been in our more than three centuries
of existence.
Let us consider what we can contribute to our world. Let us each drop a
pebble into the waters of modern discourse; thereby causing a minor ripple that
might disturb the placid waters of an apathetic society.
We are off to the races, my brethren and friends. Let’s go about repairing
our world, by improving ourselves. I pledge to walk with you on your way, if you
so promise to walk with me on mine. Let us not forget that we took an obligation
from, and to each other. May this be God’s will.
Thank you.

Report of the Senior Grand Warden
Per Capita Recommendation for 2015-2016
M. David Perry, Senior Grand Warden

Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California,
As your Senior Grand Warden, I am responsible for preparing and
presenting to the Grand Lodge a proposal for the per capita assessment that will
be collected in 2015 to fund the operations of Grand Lodge fiscal year for the
period of November 1, 2015 through October 31, 2016.
Beginning with my term as Junior Grand Warden, I have worked very
closely with the Executive Committee, the Finance Committee and the Grand
Lodge staff to develop projections of the income and the necessary expenses for
the 2015/2016 fiscal year. Earlier this year, I was able to share our plans with the
Masters and Wardens who attended our spring leadership retreats. I very much
appreciate the comments and input I received during and following the retreats.
In preparing a draft budget for the 2015/2016 fiscal year, I have considered
the factors that will increase per capita, as well as those that will mitigate any
necessary increase. The major factors that will increase the per capita are:
•
•

•

•
•
•

Membership decline. We project a total loss of 1,306 billable members.
This represents a loss in revenue of $51,587, or $1.01 in Per Capita.
Per Capita Reserve. In 2014 a Per Capita Reserve in the amount of
$34,478 was approved by the membership to be carried over into Fiscal
2014/2015. There is no reserve for 2015/2016 which affects Per Capita
by $.68.
World Conference of Grand Lodges. This extremely important conference
is being hosted by our Grand Lodge early in 2015/2016. I have included
$50,000 in this year’s Per Capita calculation to help underwrite a portion
of this conference. This represents $.98 in Per Capita.
Insurance. Premiums for our lodge insurance coverage will increase by
5.1%. This represents $.22 in Per Capita.
Personnel costs. Wages are held to a 3% increase. All other Personnel
costs will increase by an additional 5.3%. Personnel cost increases
represent $1.57 in Per Capita.
Inflation. Items subject to inflation are expected to increase by 2% to 3%.

Per Capita would need to increase by $4.95 to cover the effect of all of
these factors discussed here.
The factors that will help offset the per capita increase are the following:
•
•

Revenue Improvements. Revenue Improvements driven by an $85,000
increase in the Nob Hill Dividend significantly help offset the factors
that increase Per Capita.
Cost savings. We have identified a number of expenses that can be held
at or near last year’s levels. You will notice that the expenses in many
categories are nearly the same as the budget presented by the Deputy
Grand Master.

These factors allow us to present a balanced budget, with a per capita
assessment of $39.50. Although this represents an increase of $3.00 over the
2014/2015 assessment, it represents a modest increase of 3.7% after the cost of
the World Conference of Grand Lodges and the effect of the 2014/2015 Per Capita
Reserve are factored out. Both of these items are one‐time items.
I very much appreciate your feedback on matters that are important to
our Craft and I thank you for your support of this Per Capita proposal.

Revenue Analysis
PER CAPITA

There are several factors that affect Per Capita. Membership levels, insurance, labor
costs, professional fees and general inflation are all primary factors. The Per Capita
analysis for 2015/2016 includes a few more items than in previous years. Membership
projections show a total loss of 1,306 members which represents $51,587 or $1.01 in
Per Capita. In 2015/2016 we will be hosting the World Conference of Grand Lodges.
Support for this conference of $50,000 has been included in the budget which
represents $.98 in Per Capita. In 2014 a Per Capita Reserve in the amount of $34,478
was approved by the membership to be carried over into Fiscal 2014/2015. There is
no reserve for 2015/2016 which affects Per Capita by $.68. Insurance and labor
increases along with inflation of approximately 2% account for the additional Per
Capita. All other things being equal, the Per Capita would have to be increased by
$4.95 to cover the effect of all of these factors discussed here. Due to improvements in
Revenue driven by the Nob Hill Dividend will result in a revenue increase of $99,585, a
$1.95 reduction in Per Capita. These factors allow us to present a balanced budget
with a Per capita of $39.50.

Report of the Grand Treasurer
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The overall financial condition of your Grand Lodge continues to be
very good due to the hard work and diligent efforts of Grand Lodge officers,
boards and committee members and the efficient Grand Lodge staff.
With a strengthening economy, Grand Lodge budgets continue to be
closely monitored amid continuing efforts to conserve and curtail spending.
Your Grand Lodge Investment Committee continues their customary
diligence over the Grand Lodge’s investment portfolio. As a result of their
consideration of the current economic environment, they have made some wellstudied changes in the make-up and allocation of the portfolio in anticipation
of continued volatility in the economy and markets. They are continuing to
consider new asset classes and investment managers to further diversify our
investment portfolio.
The Investment Committee continues to recommend that no more than
4.5% of Investments be distributed to the Grand Lodge operating budget and to
the other entities participating in the investment pool. This will preserve capital in
the face of future potential inflation.
Your Grand Lodge Insurance Committee applies their considerable
expertise to the ongoing risk management of the Grand Lodge and our various
entities to keep them well-protected at favorable and competitive premium costs.
The Grand Lodge Finance Committee provides advice in the development
of the Grand Lodge operating budgets and the per capita as well as advice to
our lodges.
The Audit Committee determines who will audit our books and records
and provides tax services for the Grand Lodge and its related entities. The Audit
Committee also reviews the annual audits and 990 tax returns and provides an
independent report to the boards of each entity. This year, the Audit Committee
also reviewed the audit work that Moss Adams provides, and they have decided
to reappoint them as auditors of our Grand Lodge and our related entities. The
Committee continues to be impressed by Moss Adams’ diligence and expertise in
carrying out the audits in a cost-efficient manner.
Both the Audit and the Finance committees perform their respective
duties with business-like efficiency of which any organization would be proud.
During the past year, we have introduced the elements of good financial
management for a Lodge at our Secretaries and Treasurers Retreats, our Masters
and Wardens Retreats and at this year’s Inspector Development Academy.

110

Proceedings of the

The elements we have encouraged every Lodge and Hall Association to
have include an approved annual budget, an investment program in line with our
CMC, an annual lodge and hall association audit program using the guidelines
on our Member Center prepared by our Grand Lodge Audit Committee, up to
date tax filings for the IRS and the California Franchise Tax Board, and complete
financial and investment reporting to the Lodge and to the Grand Lodge.
I am very concerned about the status of our Lodges collective tax filings.
As an outgrowth of this year’s effort by our Grand Lodge to file the IRS and
Franchise Tax Board annual tax filings on behalf of our Lodges, our Grand Lodge
staff determined that approximately 85 of our Lodges have not stayed current
with their filing of federal and state taxes and as a result are in danger of losing
their tax exempt status. In addition to these 85 lodges there are another 35 lodges
that have already lost their Federal tax exemption. When a lodge loses their tax
exemption, they are at risk of having to pay taxes on all their income. The Grand
Lodge Finance staff is working hard to reinstate the tax exempt status of those 35
lodges who have lost their exemption.
I would like to encourage all of your Lodges to make a special effort to
be sure their taxes have been properly filed.
One way to ensure both your Lodge’s financial statements and tax filings
are done on time is to consider using Intacct, the accounting system that the
Grand Lodge introduced two years ago. Currently a total of 104 Lodges and
41 Hall Associations are using Intacct. An additional 95 Lodges and 37 Hall
Associations are using the Intacct test site preparing to utilize the system in real
time for their accounting and reporting purposes. Intacct is continually improved
by its developers and our current users are suggesting changes that will improve
the system for our Fraternity’s future use.
Two years ago, legislation was passed that allowed lodges to transfer
their Life Membership Fund to the Grand Lodge for investment. As of the end
of August, 12 lodges have transferred their life membership funds to the Grand
Lodge, totaling $ 356,464. For the Lodges who have participated since last August
1, the one year rate of return of their funds has been 10.5%.
The dedicated and efficient financial staff in the Grand Lodge office
continues to provide unexcelled service in the management and reporting on the
financial affairs of our organization under the leadership of our Chief Financial
Officer, Thomas Boyer.
You can be very proud of the work that has been done by all those
involved in the financial affairs of our fraternity. The detailed financial information
I am going to give you today is for a nine-month period from the start of this
current fiscal year, November 1, 2013, through July 31, 2014. I will compare that
information to the same period a year earlier. This report is already posted on
the Member Center under Forms/165th Annual Communication. It will continue

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

111

to be available to you until the official proceedings of this Communication
are published. Those proceedings will contain the customary audited financial
statements for the entire fiscal year.
It should be noted that this partial-year information has been prepared
internally by our fine financial staff and has not been audited.
As of July 31, 2014, your Grand Lodge had assets of $ 10,226,927 and
liabilities of $ 4,166,116 for Total Net Assets of $ 6,060,811. Total Net Assets
at the end of July were 4.7% higher than at the end of our October 31, 2013
fiscal year.
Keep in mind that most of the assets you might attach to the California
Grand Lodge are not actually owned by the Grand Lodge, itself, and do not
appear in these numbers. I am referring to assets such as this facility, which is
owned by the California Masonic Memorial Temple, our homes in Union City
and Covina which are owned by the Masonic Homes of California, the Acacia
Creek community in Union City and the California Masonic Foundation - all
separate corporations.
The investment accounts of the Grand Lodge and related entities were up
10.5% for the 12 months ending July 31, 2014. The annualized return for the prior
three year period was 8.5% and 10.0% annualized for the prior five year period.
Your Grand Lodge continues to operate in the black on a year-to-year
basis. For the nine months ending July 31, 2014, total income was $ 1,924,317
while total expenses were $1,770,226. This income was 5.4% higher than the
comparative period last year. Expenses for the nine month period ending July
31, 2014 were 7.0% higher. This increase was due primarily to a 3.5% salary/
wage increase for our Staff, employee health insurance increases of 7-8%, other
routine fraternal expense increases and the higher cost of our Grand Lodge
insurance Program.
While the Net Excess of income over expenses is $ 155,091, it should
be noted that approximately 30% of total year’s expenses are expected to occur in
the last three months of the fiscal year. The current projection, however, is that the
Grand Lodge will end this fiscal year on October 31st with a modest surplus. This
will be the seventh year in a row that Grand Lodge will have ended the year with
a small operating surplus versus the budgets you, my Brothers, have approved
each year.
The 2014 expense budget is divided in the following manner: 29.0%
for fraternal matters (such as this Annual Communication, travel expenses of
elected and appointed Grand Lodge Officers, insurance for the constituent lodges
as well as other miscellaneous fraternal expenses), 18.1% for Appropriations and
Programs (such as Leadership Development programs, various lodge support
committees, the Freemason magazine and other Committees such as Policy,

112

Proceedings of the

Jurisprudence, Investment, Ritual and Trial Review), and 52.9 % for General
and Administrative items (such as salaries and benefits, accounting and auditing,
investment management fees, legal fees and general office operations).
These results reflect the concern and diligence that the Grand Lodge
Executive Committee, the Grand Lodge Finance Committee and the Grand Lodge
financial staff bring to the monitoring of actual income and expenses versus the
budget. The numbers are compiled and studied by all parties in great detail as the
year progresses. You should know that any surplus at the end of the fiscal year is
not carried over into the next year, but instead is permanently transferred to the
Grand Lodge Endowment Fund. The result is that each Grand Master starts his
year with a zero balance with only the budget for that year to work with.
I would like to thank the many highly dedicated brothers who serve on
the various boards and committees of this Grand Lodge and its related entities for
the extraordinary amount of time, energy, dedication and hard work they devote
to the business and fraternal affairs of our California Masonic community. Please
seek them out and say “Thank You” for the work they do.
Under the capable leadership of our Grand Secretary, Very Worshipful
Allan Casalou, our Grand Lodge staff performs exceptional service for your Grand
Lodge and remains committed to offering exceptional support to our lodges and
our membership. Our Grand Lodge organization and administration is the model
among sister Grand Lodges. Please join me in thanking them.
And finally, my brethren, I thank each of you for having allowed me to
work with you and for you during this past year. I have been honored to be a part
of the California Masonic Grand Lodge team.
Respectfully submitted,
A. Raymond Schmalz, Grand Treasurer

Report of the Grand Secretary
Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge,
I am pleased to present to you this, my seventh report, as your
Grand Secretary.
Lodge and Membership Information
As of today, there are 337 chartered lodges in our jurisdiction, including
one lodge under dispensation and five research lodges. There were two lodge
consolidations during the year. Chowchilla Lodge No. 485 and Yosemite Lodge
No. 99 in Merced consolidated to form Yosemite Lodge No. 99. North County
Daylight Lodge No. 843 and Consuelo Lodge No. 325, both in Escondido,
consolidated to form Consuelo Lodge No. 325.
Our membership including Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft
Masons, at the beginning of the fiscal year was 63,054. For the 2014 fiscal year,
we had 2,587 gains and 9,809 losses. The ending membership on June 30, 2014,
was 55,875, which includes 3,945 Entered Apprentice Masons, 1,068 Fellow
Craft Masons and 50,862 Master Masons. Our database also includes 24,533
Masonic widows.
As you know, this latest membership year was the first time a Lodge was
able to suspend Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons for non-payment
of dues. There was a lot of speculation about how many of these brothers would
be suspended. We now have the results. We started the year with 10,234 Entered
Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons; 5,675 or 55% of them were suspended for
non-payment of dues. These suspensions account for the unusually high number
of losses this year.
A more detailed report of membership activity, together with a number
of Lodge by-law amendments, life memberships, and veteran’s awards is included
in my written report to be distributed in the Proceedings.
Summary of Accomplishments
There were a number of accomplishments during the year and I would
like to mention a few of them today.
Intacct and Government Returns
As you heard from the Grand Treasurer, about one-third of our lodges
are now using the Intacct system for their financial accounting and reporting. Our
Intacct team provided over 100 hours of system training for our lodge secretaries

116

Proceedings of the

and treasures this year. This training occurred one-on- and in groups. One-on-one
training happened over the phone or in person. We held seven group trainings. Two
were held at the secretaries and treasurers retreats and additional trainings were
held in Eureka, Santa Barbara, Fresno, Covina, and Vacaville. Three more are
scheduled later in this calendar year in San Diego, Palm Springs, and Sacramento.
We have a small team that has been formed to prepare and file the annual
tax returns for our lodges to help them avoid the penalties of not filing as our
Grand Treasurer explained. This year, the Grand Lodge finance team offered
this service to all lodges and 152 took us up on the offer; 137 lodges opted out
stating that they would file their own returns and 47 lodges did not respond to the
offer. Of the 152 who opted in, the Grand Lodge has successfully filed returns
for 128 lodges. We are still working on 24 lodges that have either had their taxexempt status revoked or there is another issue with their exempt status blocking
the filing of their return. We will resolve these issues and see that the returns are
filed successfully.
I want to thank all of the lodge leaders who have worked so diligently
in providing the information necessary to take on this project and I want to thank
our finance team for their excellent work. When we work together, our lodges and
our Grand Lodge, we can accomplish so much more than when we work alone.
Leadership Development
Our leadership retreats were very successful this year. For a number of
years we’ve worked to increase the number of lodges that sent attendees to the
retreats. While we were just around 50% for a long time, over the last few years
this percentage has steadily increased. This year, nine more lodges participated
than the previous year, taking the total number of lodges represented to 235 or
71% of our lodges. The retreats are facilitated by a group of dedicated Masons
who put many hours into their own development as facilitators and then volunteer
several weekends to provide the training. The facilitators this year included
Worshipful Brothers Brian Bezner, Bruce Galloway, Eric Hatfield, Marc Newman,
David Perry, James Banta, Chris Rucker, Gary Silverman, Jairo Gomez, Randy
Brill, Jeff Schimsky, David Coss, Tom Colgan, Jeff Wilkins, Jordan Yelinek, and
Brothers Doug Ismail, Andrew Uehling and Candler Gibson.
More Masons completed the Lodge Management Certification Program
this year than any of the last three years. These brothers dedicated two evening or
weekend days to a 90-minute webinar. They completed an exam at the end of the
course. A number of brothers served as instructors for these programs and I would
like to recognize them now: Gary Peterson, Shay Maghame, Jordan Yelinek, Ray
Schmalz, Eric Hatfield, Candler Gibson, John Cover Spear, James Banta, and
Marc Newman.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

117

Communications
I continue to be very proud of our communications. As you know, we
publish six issues of the California Freemason magazine in print and in digital
formats, we publish 12 issues of the electronic newsletter “The Leader” and we
publish an annual report. We maintain several websites, and utilize Facebook,
Twitter, YouTube and Instagram to communicate with our members and the
general public.
For the last eleven years, our California Freemason magazine and our
other publications have won awards from the Association of Media and Publishing.
This year we won four awards including a gold award for the best annual report.
To give you an idea of the competition – the silver award or second place award
went to Rotary International.
We are connected with nearly 65,000 people on Facebook – our network
grew by 400% this year alone. Each week, our posts reach as many as 100,000
people and about 10,000 on average are engaged each week liking, commenting,
and sharing our posts.
We maintain a digital version of the Freemason magazine on an app
called CFM – it’s available from the app stores. We have nearly 40,000 subscribers
from 158 countries. This year, the digital magazine subscriptions increased 20%
with 9,000 new subscribers from 112 countries.
The Vault
Finally, this year we launched The Vault, an online document storage
program for lodges. Driven by member demand and specification, The Vault was
created so that lodges can store minutes, applications, bylaws, and other important
documents online. We have also provided resources for lodges to organize and
store their paper documents. Nearly 80 lodges are already using The Vault, with
more joining every month.
Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges
It is my responsibility as the Grand Secretary to keep the Grand Master
informed on matters pertaining to the recognition of foreign Grand Lodges and
to present to you in the form of a motion the recognition of certain Grand Lodges
that meet our criteria therefore.
Section 409.010 of the California Masonic Code permits our Grand Lodge
to recognize any Grand Lodge that is regularly formed by lodges which trace their
origin to regular and legitimate Ancient Craft Masonry; hold undisputed sway as
the acknowledge sole or concurrent supreme power in Ancient Craft Masonry in
the territory in which they claim jurisdiction; confine their authority and exercise
thereof to the three degrees of Craft or Symbolic Masonry; and subscribe to the
General Regulations of Freemasonry.

118

Proceedings of the

We receive assistance in the evaluation of Grand Lodges seeking
recognition from the Commission on Information for Recognition, a committee
of the Conference of Grand Masters of Masons of North America. We’re honored
in California that our very own Past Grand Master, Most Worshipful Brother
William J. Bray III, is a member of that commission.
One Grand Lodge has written to our Grand Lodge seeking
mutual recognition.
The Regular Grand Lodge of Montenegro
The Regular Grand Lodge of Montenegro was legally consecrated on
May 12, 2007, by three lodges that worked under the auspices of the Regular
Grand Lodge of Yugoslavia and was chartered by the United Grand Lodges
of Germany. The consecration was performed by the United Grand Lodges of
Germany, the Grand Lodge of Serbia, the Grand Orient of Italy, and the Grand
Lodge of Austria.
It is the opinion of the Commission on Information for Recognition that
this Grand Lodge meets the requirements for recognition. Therefore I move that
the Grand Lodge of California grant mutual recognition to the Regular Grand
Lodge of Montenegro. Motion ADOPTED.
Charters and Dispensations
In accordance with §801.065 of the California Masonic Code, Destiny
Lodge U.D. in Covina has petitioned this Grand Lodge for a Charter. Grand Master
Lowe granted a dispensation to Destiny Lodge on August 30, 2013. In reviewing
the records of this Lodge and from the information provided by the District
Inspector, it has been determined that Destiny Lodge has met the requirements of
the petition. Accordingly I move that a Charter be issued to Destiny Lodge U.D.
and that it be entered into the Registry of this Grand Lodge as Destiny Lodge No.
856. Motion Adopted.
As I conclude my report, I also wish to extend my appreciation and
gratitude to the 337 lodge Secretaries and 176 Assistant Secretaries in this
jurisdiction whose dedicated work is the backbone of our lodges and of our Grand
Lodge. I also wish to thank our Assistant Grand Lecturers and District Inspectors
who, in addition to their Ritual duties, work very diligently on a number of
administrative matters throughout the year.

I work with a number of Grand Lodge committees that perform essential

for at least one year. Worshipful Brother Rob Scott has been the chairman of the

with their dedicated service. I thank them all for their commitment and good work.
I want to recognize one of our longest-tenured team members. As a young man,
Brother Richard Gentschel was a part of the crew that installed the original sound

You have noticed by now that I am operating this weekend without

Grand Lodge.
Lastly, I want to thank our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Brother John
L. Cooper III, who has been a friend and mentor to me for more than fifteen years.
I’m sure I speak for all the brethren, Most Worshipful, when I thank you for your
leadership as our Grand Master. So many of us were a part of and witnessed
the programs and initiatives that you continued or established this year and this
work will have a lasting impact on our fraternity, surpassed only by your personal
impact on our hearts and minds. Our Grand Master is probably one of the most
interesting students on the subject of Freemasonry. For fifty years now, Most
Worshipful Cooper has been reading and writing about Freemasonry, which has
surely contributed to the man he is today and the example he sets for us as he

brings Masonic values and ideals to his every act and word. As I observed him

145

Report of the Grand Lecturer
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
Our Code requires the Grand Lecturer to render to Grand Lodge, at each
Annual Communication, a full and detailed account of his services during the
year, and to set forth, with respect to ritual, the condition of the Lodges. Therefore,
I offer the following report.
It has been a pleasure and a very high honor to serve you as Grand
Lecturer this year and it is a memory that I will cherish for the rest of my life.
A Full and Detailed Account of My Services During the Year
In support of our Grand Master’s theme, “Freemasonry: Our Moral
Compass” and the goal four Fraternity’s strategic plan to increase the relevance of
our fraternity and enhance the member experience, I have worked to remind our
Brethren that our ritual is, in fact, the foundation of our fraternity and therefore the
basis upon which our individual moral compasses are built. Such a belief allows
us to be civil to each other through a willingness to understand, accept and work
with the uniqueness of each Brother’s talents and personality.
My work this year continued to reinforce the philosophy that our ritual
remains relevant in our lives and makes us more successful both as individuals
and as lodges.
Our ritual provides each candidate and raised Master Mason with an
enriched environment within which he may work to progress beyond the basic
Masonic catechisms and into higher levels of consciousness that, in turn, has a
profound effect on not only the individual Brother but also on those around him,
his family, lodge and community.
As I traveled throughout the state I continued my practice of highlighting
the history behind our ritual by using specially prepared posters strategically
placed on various lodge paraphernalia to promote an interest to search out the
meanings behind our paraphernalia; some of which are provided to us when
installed and others through independent research such as:
•

The Marshal’s baton as a symbol of “command” is taught to us during
the Installation ceremony, while

•

The Stewards’ white rods as symbols of “purity” and “innocence,” and

•

The Deacon’s blue rods as symbols of “friendship” and “benevolence”
are learned through independent research and education.

146

Proceedings of the

Those posters served as a method to stir the interest of those who arrived
early at my Master Mason seminars as well as support for my introductory remarks
regarding our ritual’s history. It should be noted that those posters duplicated
information I previously placed into the Inspector’s library for their use with the
officers and members of the lodges within their respective Districts.
In support of the strategically placed posters, I placed additional posters
in the East to reinforce my discussion on developing and strengthening a culture
of ritual excellence. These posters discussed the following issues:
•

The culture of Masonic instruction;

•

Attitude Precedes behavior;

•

Importance of history;

•

Development of personal connections;

•

Developing a tradition of excellence;

•

Ritual also supports a shared purpose (teamwork, respect for others,
esteem building, and leadership development);

•

We are not alone (the importance of working together);

•

Our beliefs infect others; and

•

All factors must coalesce to form a culture.

During each degree exemplification I also took the opportunity to insert
historical references as a way to make it easier to remember why something was
being done and to reinforce the importance of ensuring a presentation that was
accomplished with understanding, feeling, and an abundance of care for each
other and especially for the candidate.
To enhance the member experience I prepared a set of guidelines, that
was approved by the Ritual Committee and the Grand Master, that will allow a
lodge, on an annual basis and under strict supervision of the District Inspector,
to confer a degree in the dining room in a manner similar to what our forefathers
did in the days before there were purpose-built lodge rooms when they met,
socialized, ate, conferred a degree, and resumed eating and socializing until they
closed their meeting.
To Set Forth, With Respect to Ritual, the Condition of the Lodges
This year I supervised two Inspector ritual seminars, which included a
town hall meeting between the Inspectors and the Grand Master, which was also
attended by the Deputy Grand Master, and included instruction on introduction

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

147

protocols, and the exemplifications of all three degrees. Additionally, I supervised
five Master Masons seminars where the Fellow Craft Degree was exemplified in
Divisions 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 with several Divisions also inviting attendance by
lodges in neighboring Divisions.
In general I can say that delivery of our ritual, aided by the Inspector’s
testing of the proposed Ritual Floor Work Manual, has become more consistent
and in many cases well performed. I have also noticed that some lodges have
yet to take ownership of the quality of their ritual, choosing to accept a tradition
of mediocrity that negatively affects their administrative as well as social
activities. It is my aspiration that the work done by the Ritual Committee and
Inspectors with the Craft will inspire those later lodges to see the benefits of an
improved ritual environment and rekindle a commitment to ritual excellence.
To assist in further improving our ritual the Ritual Committee will
sponsor another ritual completion in 2015, this time on the 2nd Section of the 3rd
Degree where the best degree team from each Division will be honored. A formal
announcement and registration from will be distributed soon.Before I conclude
my report I want to thank three Brothers. This year the Ritual Committee says
goodbye to three Assistant Grand Lecturers: Worshipful Bruce Galloway,
Worshipful Cline “Cub” Jack and Worshipful Frank Lee.
To each of them I say thank you for all your service to the Craft in general
and to the Ritual Committee in particular. We wish them future success as they
continue their work in the vineyards of Freemasonry.
I wish to extend personal recognition to Worshipful Frank Lee for his
outstanding support and loyalty throughout the years. Frank always worked above
and beyond the call of duty in support the Ritual Committee’s efforts. I wish
to thank him for his efforts to ensure the accuracy of the upcoming ritual floor
work manual as well as the production of a DVD training film on how to plan
and present a Grand Lodge cornerstone ceremony. Frank will have this DVD
completed and ready for your use by the end of the year.
Frank, I thank you for your past contributions to our Craft and look
forward to your future service and success.
Finally, I have participated in the continuing efforts by a taskforce
created last year by Most Worshipful Lowe and currently being chaired by RW
Russ Charvonia. This Taskforce on Ritual is exploring future methods to improve
our ritual instruction with the goal to have qualified officers performing quality
ritual so that the degree experience is deeply meaningful to all candidates, and that
all members consider their experience to be rewarding.
This concludes my report. Thank you.
Respectfully submitted,
Jack M. Rose, Grand Lecturer

Grand Chaplain’s Message

by The Very Reverend Leonard B. Oakes
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Right Worshipful Sir, Very Worshipful
Sirs, Most Worshipful Past Grand Masters, Worshipful Sirs, Brethren, Friends,
Ladies and Gentlemen, let me first greet you all with a warm symbolic embrace.
Please keep that with you and remember that you have entered into a wider family
of love in this beautiful, magnificent and historic Grand Lodge in the heart of San
Francisco, a city set on a hill and certainly the highest hill in San Francisco with a
Grand Lodge of Masons in California standing tall!
It is still quite a wonder for me to be standing tall here before you, just
like those who have done before me, with great humility, to be of service to all
great people that uphold the great principles of Masonry, brotherly love, relief,
and truth. God must have touched the heart of John and Heather and called me to
be part of service, part of growing and part of further understanding the lights of
masonry. Such calling reminds me of a joke:
A husband and wife were concerned that their son was not getting up on
a Sunday morning. The Husband asked his wife to go check in with him.
She knocked at his door and whispered, “Son it’s 8:00 on Sunday
morning, aren’t you going to Church today?” The son opened the door and said,
“I am not going to that church for two reasons: First, they don’t like me, second,
I don’t like them either.” To which the mother replied, “Son, I will tell you two
reasons why you must go to church today: First, you are 59 years old, and second,
you are the priest!”
I compare that to how I was called to this humble Grand Lodge office as
a Chaplain. John and Heather met with my wife Haidee and me over dinner. John
said, “God has called you to a wider calling, to be my Grand Chaplain.” I must
say, after many excuses, I said, “yes!”
Freemasonry is full of wonder and love. You will never know what
happens when you say, “yes”. It will take you to new places, introduce you to new
friends and help develop great relationships. It makes one, a better person with
a broader perspective. Most importantly, it gives you wider vision of one’s self,
weaved to the needs of others with compassion, and love taking them up to a new
level of life. You see, we are all called to service for a reason, at the right time, in
the perfect moment. We are called from different backgrounds, yet we treat each
other to be on the level. That is Masonry in action.
Someone asked me, “What is a priest like you doing in Masonry?” I
replied with two reasons; first, to seek further light in the brotherhood of man, and
secondly, God has called me to widen my tent and be the light among many lights
in God’s beautiful tapestry of families, communities and nations.

152

Proceedings of the

Contrary to what the conspiracy theorists say and those who try to
discredit Freemasonry, Freemasonry, is not a religion and is not a substitute for
religion. Let there be no mistake about this. While a belief in God is a prerequisite
for a man to become a Mason, he must have his own relationship with God outside
the context of Freemasonry. We do not have a theology, we do not lead anyone to
a relationship with his God, and we do not in any way ask a man to substitute his
own understanding of God, as taught by his particular religious faith, for anything
he will learn in Freemasonry. Freemasonry deals with our relationships with each
other, and the implications that such relationships have on our own lives, and
the lives of those we meet along the pathway of life. We insist that a man is
responsible before his God for what he does with his life, but we ask each one
to seek the important and eternal answers from his own religious faith. That is
what makes freemasonry alive. Even today, there is sheer respect in each other’s
faith, knowing that we are ever walking upon the level of time and are all equal
in the eyes of God and so with our dealings with each other. Thus, Freemasonry
continue to exist in every clime and country, in every profession and in every
walk of life.
There are things that I learned as a priest and a Grand Chaplain that I
would like to leave with you as leaders in the free world:
First, I ask you to see things in the eyes of God. Let us look at freemasonry
with an eye that sees possibility. All things are possible with the all seeing-eye and
so we must learn to look for the hidden possibility when things seem impossible.
We must look with God’s eyes.
We all know that when things get tough, fear creeps in. We all have our
own personal experiences with fear, in our work and in our lodges. In our role as
leaders and as lodge officers, we worry that there won’t be enough money, enough
time, enough volunteers or members to keep things going. Fear comes from our
sense of scarcity. There is not enough, there is never enough. We cannot do what
we need to do. Fear blinds us to opportunity and kills our creativity. When fear
creeps in always remember these words; God always gives enough to accomplish
what he has asked us to do. God is a generous giver, never stingy. If God has
asked us to do something, then whatever he has dreamed for us is possible and the
resources are available, if we search them out. Seeing with God’s eyes is the first
practice we should all do, especially in these times.
The second is Prayer, believe in the power of prayer. We all must be
anchored with prayers, by putting down a few anchors in our days and weeks
to center us in turbulent waters. We all know what it feels like to be pushed and
pulled and swept up in a hard day or week. When the going gets tough in our
deliberations of business in the lodge, sometimes we just go from thing to thing,
never reflecting on what we are doing or where we are. Leaders now would do
well to remember this ancient practice for anchoring themselves in the turbulent
seas of life with regular prayer. It sounds simple but there is truth about many of
us don’t really “make the time” for this practice and get swept out to sea when the
going gets tough.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

153

A daily prayer time helps us to consecrate and bless each day. Whether
we take the time for a 30 minute meditation each morning or simply 2 minutes at
the end of the day offer God a silent prayer about how I find myself today. Regular
prayer time is an anchor to keep us centered, and leaders in these times need to
be centered. I know that when I take even 5 minutes in the morning, or in the
space of a busy work day to offer a prayer to God or sit quietly with God, my next
decisions and actions are more balanced and less reactive. The harder our days
and meetings become, the more we need this anchor of regular time to connect
with God and ourselves. It helps us stay centered in our meetings. Prayer matters,
it can be a personal anchor and it can anchor you as a leader, as well.
Believe in the power of prayer. Even an Atheist know how to pray:
An atheist was walking through the woods one day, admiring all that
God had created. “What majestic trees! What a powerful river! What beautiful
animals!” he said to himself. As he was walking alongside the river, he heard a
rustling in the bushes behind him.
Turning to look, he saw a 13-foot Grizzly bear beginning to charge
towards him. He ran as fast as he could down the path.
He looked over his shoulder and saw that the bear was rapidly closing on
him. Somehow, he ran even faster, so scared that tears came to his eyes. He looked
again & the bear was even closer. His heart pounding in his chest, he tried to run
faster yet. But alas, he tripped and fell to the ground.
As he rolled over to pick himself up, the bear was right over him,
reaching for him with it’s left paw and raising its right paw to strike him....he
yelled out, “oh my god!”
Time stopped.......The bear froze.......The forest was silent............Even
the river stopped moving.
Suddenly, a thunderous voice came from the heavens.
God spoke:
“You deny my existence for all these years, teach others that I don’t exist
now, do you expect me to help you out of this predicament? Am I to count you
now as a believer?”
Bewildered, the atheist looked directly into the sky & said, “It would be
hypocritical to ask to be a Christian after all these years, but perhaps you could
make the bear a Christian?”
“Very well,” said God.
The light went out...The river ran...The sounds of the forest resumed..
And the bear dropped down on his knees, brought both paws together,
bowed his head and spoke:

154

Proceedings of the

“Lord, thank you for this food which I am about to receive from your
bounty. Amen.” And all the Masons say? (So mote it be)
Let us consecrate each day with the anchor of prayer and invite prayer
into our meetings to bless our work. We look with the eyes of God, sure to find
the loaves that God calls us to bless break and share in a hungry world. These
practices are gifts from God to us. Try them and they will bless your family, your
personal life, your leadership and your organizations abundantly.
May God bless the Grand Lodge of California, this nation and the world.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

155

Session Prayers
Rededication Ceremony
Great Architect and Ruler of the Universe! We most reverently invoke
Thy blessing on this memorable occasion. We remember and thank Thee, for the
vision of our Brethren, who pledged their faith, dedication and integrity to the
renovation and revitalization of this auditorium. May the pledges of our Brethren
in the past and present inspire those in the future. Continue to bless all who come
through the doors of this auditorium. May their pursuits be fulfilling and may
they be touched by the Masonic ideals expressed in the art and architecture of this
edifice. And to thee we shall ascribe all the honor and glory forever. Amen.
Saturday Morning
Ever-loving God, you have brought us together and empowered us to
serve as your people. We ask you to guide and bless us as we strive to tell the
Good News of your love; teach and nurture families and communities; tend to the
human condition; transform and reconcile the world by your love; and treasure
your creation and our salvation. May we be engulfed in your love and blessings
as we live out the mission and work you have given us, in your most loving name
we pray. Amen.

accomplish the business of the day. Let harmony and peace envelope us so that
we may glorify your name in all our doings. Amen.

Most loving and gracious God, our great provider, after such great

continue to bestow upon us. We ask you now to be in our midst and be part of our
joy and sharing so that we may be more inspired to do the works you have set for

love and that we may always be knit together in the spirit of unity. We invite you

the night who will accompany us in our sleep so that we may welcome again a
new day, a new grace with your love. Amen.

Loving God, our Heavenly Father, we thank you for the spirit of unity

Grand Oration

The Crossroads of a Mason
Most Worshipful Sir and Brethren all:
In my travels throughout this year, which has included conversations with
many of you, I have discovered something that is fundamentally important: each
Mason comes to a crossroads in Freemasonry. Does he casually take the obligation
and maintain his current status quo or does he strive to truly understand and apply
the exceptional components of our craft? Our teachings provide a foundation for
each Mason’s life, which guides his overall conduct. The foundations of our ritual
– our Masonic teachings – are having the impact that they were intended to have.
Our members are more aware that their words and actions impact how we are
viewed as individuals and as members of Freemasonry.
Our members are committing to our craft and have a growing desire
for education to understand the ritual on a deeper level. Our candidates are
seeking a deeper connection to what it means to be a Freemason today. There is
a thirst for more scholarly works on the history of Masonry. There is a surge in
understanding the subtle points of our ritual that are more profound than we might
think, such as the geometric shape that is formed with the rods of the Senior and
Junior Deacons at the altar. Focusing on all parts of our ritual and how they fit
together is paramount to understanding our heritage from operative Masons and
our connection to a Supreme Being. As is set forth in our first degree lecture,
“When the whole building was completed its several parts fitted together with
such exact nicety that it had more the appearance of the work of the Supreme
Architect of the Universe than that of Human Hands.” Our needs are the same as
those of our earliest brothers—they were seeking something that was not found
in their daily lives – beyond the church, their career, and their status in society.
They were looking for something that would lead them on a path of completeness.
There was a need to be part of something that would allow them to be with likeminded individuals. We all come to the fraternity looking for similar things.
Our first experience in the Lodge is our initiation. Each of us must
understand that, although we have advanced through the degrees, the lessons
imparted during the first degree are to remain with us. Once we have been passed
to the degree of Fellow Craft and are raised to the degree of Master Mason, we
tend to forget what we have learned in preceding degrees. We must be mindful
that no matter how long we have been part of this fraternity we are continually
striving to meet the guidelines given to us as an Entered Apprentice Mason.
The lessons, obligation, and duties of the first degree might seem the
easiest to meet, but they seem to be the hardest for us to practice on a daily basis.
As a DeMolay, I was given a set of seven precepts that I was to use to govern my
actions on a regular basis. I might not have been the best at consistently practicing
all of them. But, I would tell myself, “It’s okay, I am just a kid.” We are men.

160

Proceedings of the

As Masons, we are not allowed to pick and choose the virtues we practice. We
all took the same obligation and, although it might be hard, we must practice
Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth. We must govern our actions agreeably to the
dictates of Temperance, Fortitude, Prudence, and Justice.
The best way to apply that which you have learned is to internalize those
teachings rather than just regurgitating them. Memorizing ritual is something
that all of us have done and, for some, it comes easier than others, but do we
understand it? I recall that my eighth grade English teacher, Mrs. Davis, made
us memorize the poem, Oh Captain, My Captain by Walt Whitman. Once we
memorized it, we were to recite it to the class for a grade. It was a very easy task
for me. It was not until four years later, when I was a senior in High School that I
learned the poem was about Abraham Lincoln and appreciated the meaning. Even
if we are able to memorize and recite our ritual, it is important that we understand
what we are saying. Also, when we internalize our ritual it becomes a part of us.
As a result, it is much easier to apply and practice.
Internalizing the ritual requires each one of us to practice our virtues
on a daily basis with Masons and Non-Masons. Practicing our virtues with other
Masons should not be difficult because we are well aware that we cannot fake our
way through a fraternal interaction the way we might on a job interview or first
date. Unfortunately, we are not always mindful of practicing our virtues with all
Masons. We often fall into the trap of catering more to those holding leadership
positions within our fraternity, because human instinct dictates that we should
be looking to improve our own positions. We might ask ourselves, “What can
this person do for me in the future?” and/or “How can they help me to gain such
notoriety and distinction?” The truth is that we are all here for each other. The
actions of one Mason, good or bad, reflect on every single one of us. Just as we
don’t get to pick and choose which tenets and virtues we practice, we don’t get to
pick and choose which Masons we practice them with. The same holds true for
those who are not Masons. We must practice our tenets and virtues with all people.
We may never get a second chance to perform a kind deed, say hello, or just smile.
Common courtesy implies that all of those things are expected of us. It doesn’t
matter that those people might know that we are Masons. Masonry has given us
a foundation to practice what is right and a place to understand the importance of
doing good at all times. It is our responsibility to show that to the world.
In addition to understanding the teachings of Freemasonry, we must
engage our members as officers and key figures within the lodge regardless of
their length of time in the fraternity. I like to call this guided ambition. Most of
our current Lodge Masters have been Master Masons for only 5 years! This means
that these men were initiated into their lodges and jumped right into positions
of leadership. This could be that the lodge was in need of officers or it could
be that the individual was inspired to get involved quickly. Millennials, as they
are affectionately referred to, have ambition and believe that they can take on
anything. Ambition and belief are great things if they are guided in a positive

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

161

direction. We cannot let these young Masons accept more responsibility than they
can handle. It is admirable that they want to be involved in the various service and
philanthropic components of our Craft. It is great that they want to go through
the line as quickly as possible to become a leader of the lodge. It is praiseworthy
that they want to be involved with as much as possible at the lodge, district,
division, and Grand Lodge level. However, misguided youth and ambition can
lead to disaster, burnout, and the loss of talent that, properly honed, could return
dividends for years to come.
In order to find this kind of talent and ambition, it is important that you
show interest in the visitors to your lodge in order to see if Masonry is actually
what they are seeking. When an individual comes to your lodge and states that
he would like to become a Mason, you should take an interest and ask questions.
Does he want to become a Mason because he watched National Treasure or read
Angels and Demons and thought, “I want to do that?” Or has he reached a point
in his life where he feels that there is something missing and his research has led
him to Masonry? Our current membership is far more knowledgeable regarding
Masonry than previous generations due to the amount of information that is
accessible electronically. We must be aware of the information the visitor has and
determine whether our fraternity has what they are looking for.
Ultimately, it is important that we focus on the quality of our membership
rather than the quantity. If we are a group of men of the highest quality, others
will want to join us. Since I joined Masonry, the one committee that I wish was
no longer necessary is trial review. This has nothing to do with the brothers that
serve on the committee or their completed work. It is because somewhere along
the way we de-valued our fraternity and our teachings. We may have failed in our
investigation of a prospect to determine whether he is a man of right mind and
right intentions. As Masons, we must treat our lodge and our fraternity as our own
family. Those of you who are married are well aware of the vetting process that
takes place when evaluating a potential mate. For some, it might be more detailed
and involved than it is for others, but it is present. The overarching concern in
the vetting process is whether there is trust on both sides and how that trust can
be maintained. When we are charged with investigating a potential member of
our fraternity, we should recall the importance of trust. We can ill afford to have
a member who brings harm into our lodge. We must remember our first entrance
into the lodge to avoid bringing anything offensive or defensive into the lodge
whereby its peace and harmony would be disturbed. This will make our lodges
safe places to practice our ritual and strengthen fraternal bonds without suspicion.
When we focus on quality, both sides win.
As trustful members of Freemasonry, each of us must be proud that we
are Masons. We must develop the ability to discuss our fraternity with others,
highlighting our own passion for it. We should never fear telling others we belong
to this fraternity. When asked why we belong, we should be able to discuss the
merits of the fraternity in general. More importantly, we should be able to explain

162

Proceedings of the

the merits of the fraternity for us specifically. Conveying someone else’s passion
or using someone else’s words as your own is easy. Exhibiting your own passion
for the fraternity that has given you so much and continues to do so on a regular
basis takes deep reflection. As you go into the world outside of our lodges and you
find yourself wearing a Masonic lapel pin, you should be able to explain what it
means to you expressing your own passion.
One of the merits of our fraternity about which I am proud is our collective
strength in helping our members and our communities. Earlier this year, I spoke
at the dedication of a baseball field and emphasized teamwork. There is a belief
in our present-day society that there is no longer a need for teamwork or worse
that there is no place for it. We have become a society of individuals who think
that assistance from others isn’t necessary because they are able to do things on
their own. Even when we are given assistance from someone else to meet a goal,
we often fail to give proper credit. Our lodges and our fraternity are a team, and
it is our collective strength that allows us to be of assistance to so many people
throughout the state, the country, and the world. It is our ability to work as a team
that allows us to achieve the level of success that we have in our programs. When
we understand our individual strengths and weaknesses we are able to be a more
collaborative force. By connecting ourselves based on these individual traits we
are able to achieve the best possible outcome and cements our collective strength.
As each Mason continues to face this Crossroads, let us always be mindful
of our obligations. We should be guided by what we are as an organization and
what we want to be remembered for as individuals. Coach Yurak was my religion
teacher during my senior year of high school. I went to an all-boys school, so he
would often discuss our individual legacy. He would ask the class, “What kind of
legacy do you want to leave in this world?” Some people believe that leaving a
legacy is simply passing on the family name. However, Coach Yurak and I were
each blessed with two daughters. We understand that our legacy is not in a name
but in the character of the children that we build. This has everything to do with
how we act during our lives and has nothing to do with our names. Integrity is
based on our actions when nobody is there to see it. Our character is guided by
our obligations that we make with our fraternal brothers, with our families, and
with our friends. We made these obligations, we know what they are, and we
must follow-through. Idle obligations mean little to all that hear them especially
ourselves—never promise anything you cannot deliver. Your legacy is more than
your name, and our obligations are more than just words. The opportunity to
strengthen our fraternity is within each of us, the opportunity to strengthen our
communities is within each of us, and the opportunity to strengthen ourselves is
within each one of us and it starts today. Above all, my brothers, the path we take
on this crossroads will ensure an individual and organizational legacy.
Respectfully submitted,
Brian P. Bezner Grand Orator
