Resolution No. 14-15
Restoration of Antranik Jabourian to Masonic Membership
The proponents of this Resolution seek to restore Antranik Jabourian to
membership in Masonry.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic Code
provides that a Mason who has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere to, or has been
convicted of, a crime of moral turpitude by a federal or state court shall be deemed
automatically expelled from membership in any Lodge in this Jurisdiction without
any further action of his Lodge or Grand Lodge; and
WHEREAS, Antranik Jabourian was automatically expelled from
membership in this Jurisdiction because Antranik Jabourian pled no contest to
and was convicted of a violation of California Penal Code Section 502(c)(1) and
California Health and Safety Code Section 44059, involving smog device testing
fraud, on June 30, 1997 (collectively, the “Crime”); and

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

255

WHEREAS, on November 9, 2010, the charges against Antranik
Jabourian were dismissed under California Penal Code Section 1203.4 because
Antranik Jabourian had fulfilled the conditions of his probation; and
WHEREAS, Antranik Jabourian may be restored to membership in
Masonry only by a resolution presented and adopted using the same procedure as
an amendment to the Ordinances of Grand Lodge; and
WHEREAS, the conviction of Antranik Jabourian for smog fraud in
1997 was due to the actions of one of his employees, and Antranik Jabourian
accepted responsibility for his employee’s actions as the owner of the business
with the license being in his name, as a result of which his smog license was
suspended for one year and he was given three years’ probation; and
WHEREAS, Mr. Jabourian continued to operate his mechanic business
for many years successfully until the sale of it in 2010; and
WHEREAS, Mr. Jabourian has continuously demonstrated his upright
conduct, exemplary character, as well as good moral reputation in the community
and the fraternity, Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California 193, San Marino Lodge
No. 408, Ararat Lodge No. 848 and to the Masonic community as a whole; and
WHEREAS, his expulsion from Masonry did not deter him from
assisting the needs of the Lodge and its members; and
WHEREAS, he has always been available to help and assist any public
activities of San Marino Lodge No. 408 and Ararat Lodge No. 848 resulting
in very high regard and respect from its members as well as members of other
Lodges in Southern California; and
WHEREAS, Mr. Jabourian became a Mason on May 23, 2007 in San
Marino Lodge No. 408 and later affiliated with Ararat Lodge No. 848, becoming
a life member in both Lodges.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that, any provision of the
California Masonic Code to the contrary notwithstanding, Antranik Jabourian be
restored to the rights and benefits of Masonry as of the date of his expulsion as
an unaffiliated Mason, with no lapse in membership, and that he no longer be
subject to expulsion from Masonry under the California Masonic Code because of
the Crime.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to restore Mr. Antranik
Jabourian to membership in our Fraternity. Mr. Jabourian was expelled from
all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant to the automatic expulsion
provision of the California Masonic Code section 1410.820 as of January 1,

256

Proceedings of the

2007. Mr. Jabourian pled no contest to a violation of California Penal Code
section 502 (c) (1) and the California Health and Safety Code section 44059 on
June 30, 1997. Mr. Jabourian subsequently applied for the Degrees of Masonry
in San Marino Lodge No. 408 on November 1, 2006 and applied for Affiliation
in Ararat Lodge #848. In his initial application for membership, Mr. Jabourian
indicated that he had never been arrested, taken into custody, pleaded guilty or
nolo contendere to, or been convicted of, a criminal offence (other than a minor
traffic violation). He was elected to membership in San Marino Lodge No. 408.
CMC section 1040.1050 details the technical steps required for
reinstatement of an expelled member. For the Grand Lodge to properly assess
whether an expelled member should be reinstated, it needs to consider whether
the individual has been rehabilitated from his criminal offenses and is again
worthy of being a member of our Craft. The court dismissed the charges against
Mr. Jabourian on November 9, 2010 as he fulfilled the conditions of probation;
however, the untrue statement on his application for the Degrees of Masonry
does not appear to have not been corrected or resolved. This Resolution, as
presented, does not provide any details regarding how the expelled member
has rehabilitated himself.
As a point of reference, courts in California have ruled that rehabilitation
is a “state of mind,” and “the law looks with favor upon rewarding with the
opportunity to serve, one who has achieved ‘reformation and regeneration.’”
Fully acknowledging the wrongfulness of past actions is an essential step
towards rehabilitation.
Cases authorizing reinstatement to a professional practice on the basis
of rehabilitation typically involve a substantial period of exemplary conduct
following the applicant’s misdeeds. The more serious the misconduct and the
bad character evidence, the stronger the applicant ‘s showing of rehabilitation
must be. In determining whether to grant an application, the commonsense
notion is that rehabilitation cannot be determined separate and apart from the
offenses from which one claims to be rehabilitated. Where a high degree of
moral turpitude was involved in the misconduct, the evidence must show the
petitioner is essentially no longer the same person who behaved so poorly in
the past.
It is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this Grand
Lodge for an expelled man to apply for reinstatement. However, it is up to Grand
Lodge to determine if the man has made adequate rehabilitation.
Report of the Committee on Trial Review:
Resolution 14-15 seeks to restore Antranik Jabourian to Masonic
membership. Mr. Jabourian was automatically expelled in 2012 by virtue of his
felony convictions in the Los Angeles County Superior Court for perjury and
smog device testing fraud.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

257

Review of the court docket indicates that Mr. Jabourian was charged
on April 24, 1997; on May 30, 1997 he pled guilty to the two felonies and on
November 29, 2010, the Court dismissed the convictions pursuant to Penal
Code §1203.4 and also determined that the two convictions were to be deemed
misdemeanors for all purposes.
The proponents now seek to have him restored based on the dismissal
of the convictions and because of his good works since his expulsion. As to the
dismissal, the Masonic Code specifically provides that when a brother is convicted
of a crime of moral turpitude his - “Expulsion is automatic, irrespective of an order granting
probation following such conviction, suspending the imposition
of penalty, or of a subsequent order allowing such person to
withdraw his plea of guilty and to enter a plea of not guilty,
or setting aside the plea or verdict of guilty, or dismissing the
accusation or information, unless, for the reason that he did not
commit the offense, he either has been pardoned or has had his
judgment of conviction vacated or reversed [Emphasis added]”
As such, the dismissal by the Court is not a ground for restoration
to membership.
The Committee, in performing its duty to investigate the request,
obtained a copy of Mr. Jabourian’s application for degrees, which he submitted
on November 1, 2006, almost ten years after the conviction. He did not disclose
the two felony convictions on the application.
Beyond that, the proponents state some compelling reasons for Mr.
Jabourian to be reinstated, namely, his continued assistance to his lodges.
However, it is the opinion of the Committee that that is outweighed by the fact
that he failed to disclose the convictions at the time of his application. Were he
reinstated charges could immediately be filed again for the misrepresentation
made on the application. As such, a restoration in this case would just lead to a
trial which would not do Mr. Jabourian nor the lodges involved any good.
The Committee therefore recommends a no vote on the resolution.

§804.620. ADVANCEMENT.
A Lodge may advance an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft to a higher degree
only if:
A.

He has given satisfactory evidence, by examination in a tiled Lodge, that
he is proficient and well qualified in the degrees which he has already
taken. To demonstrate such proficiency, an Entered Apprentice or Fellow
Craft shall only be required to recite from memory the obligation of each
degree, together with the signs and modes of recognition of each degree.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit the use of the on-line
Candidate Learning Center to complete the Basic Masonic Education Course
in the degrees. The Candidate Learning Center is a tool available on the Grand
Lodge website.
This resolution will amend California Masonic Code Section 804.620
which requires candidates for degree advancement to complete written answers
from pamphlets of the Basic Masonic Education Course.
Candidates and members expect education and training to be delivered
by twenty-first century means such as on-line classes and webinars. This
resolution will provide an option of completing the course using the on-line
Candidate Learning Center.
This resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of
this Grand Lodge.

Resolution No. 14-17
Clarifies Duties of Lodge Secretary and Treasurer

The proponents of this Resolution seek to define clearly the differences in
reporting duties of the Secretary and Treasurer for the Annual and Semi-Annual
Reports to the Lodge.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, members are entitled to clear reports on the financial and
membership status of their lodge on a regular basis; and
WHEREAS, accurate and timely financial and membership records and
reporting is essential for good management of resources and governance of the
lodge; and
WHEREAS, the Annual and Semi-Annual Reports of the Secretary and
Treasurer are often duplicates; and
WHEREAS, these duplicate reports in no way enhance the management
of resources or the governance of the Lodge.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 805.220 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§805.220. DUTIES OF TREASURER.
It shall be the duty of the Treasurer to:
A.

Receive all monies from the Secretary and shall keep an accurate and
just account thereof, giving his receipt therefor, and shall pay the same
out only when an order is duly signed by the Master, countersigned by
the Secretary, and approved by vote of the Lodge;

B.

Safely keep all monies, property and other assets of the Lodge, except
to the extent they are entrusted to the Lodge Trustees by resolution,
disburse or transfer the same, or any part thereof, upon the order of the
Master, duly attested by the Secretary with the approval of the Lodge;

C.

Keep a book or books wherein a correct account of his receipts and
disbursements shall be exhibited in detail, accounting for sources of
income and expenditures, and all monies, property and other assets of
the Lodge;

D.

Report Present to the Lodge at each the Stated Meeting in August a
comprehensive statement of the Lodge’s income and expenditures,
assets and liability, on a form promulgated by the Grand Master, and

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

261

February of each year for the six month period ending on the preceding
June 30th and present at each February Stated Meeting a similar statement
for the twelve month period ending on the preceding December 31st,
respectively; and
E.

Perform such other duties, appertaining to his office, as the Bylaws of the
Lodge or this Code may require or the Lodge may direct.

The Lodge may at any time when considered necessary cause the Treasurer to
present an account of his receipts and disbursements, and of monies, property and
other assets of the Lodge on hand.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 805.230 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of Resolution 14-17 are concerned about the content of
the semi-annual and annual Secretary’s and Treasurer’s reports. Their observation
is that the two reports are often duplicative and there is no standardization from
lodge to lodge. California Masonic Code Section 805.220 (D) does require the

264

Proceedings of the

Treasurer to make such reports but does not contain any details about what
he is to tell the lodge. CMC Section 805.230 (B) does provide more specific
directives for the Secretary, in particular income, expenditures, assets, and
liabilities. The Secretary is responsible for keeping records regarding monies
transmitted to him, but our Code also seems to be requiring him to report on
investments or other holdings for which he has no direct contact during the year.
Thus, it is not surprising that the two reports are often duplicative.
If Resolution 14-17 passes, both sections of our Code will be changed.
The Secretary will report on membership activity and only on the monies that
are paid to his office directly. The Treasurer will present a broader report on the
overall financial status of the lodge.
This resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of
this Grand Lodge.
Resolution ADOPTED.

Report of the President of the Board
Masonic Homes of California
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A.M. of California:
The Masonic Homes of California provides services to California
Freemasons and their families and we recognize the importance of providing care
and support over the continuum of our members’ lives. As our fraternity continues
to evolve and our demographics continue to shift, we continue to expand and
enhance services to meet those needs in both our residential and community
based programs.
This has been a truly exciting year for the Masonic Homes. In late
October, Gary Charland, a past Board Member and a Past Master of AcalanesFellowship Lodge # 480, accepted the position of Executive Vice President. We
then embarked upon a new Campus Master Planning process, following our
February Board Retreat. This process, which will be completed in December of
this year, will allow us to position the Masonic Homes as a leader in providing
services to our Brothers, their wives and widows.
As part of our ongoing efforts to provide care for our members, we are
looking to develop the flatlands that lie in the front of our Masonic Homes in Union
City. This 63 acre parcel, currently used for growing hay, is a vital part of our long
range plan for meeting the needs of our fraternity for both short and long term
care as well as a state of the art Memory Care Facility. This property is currently
restricted by an ordinance passed by the Union City voters in the 1990’s which
was part of an effort to protect the hills of Union City from further development.
Our property is on the flatlands. We have therefore placed an initiative on the
November ballot asking the residents of Union City to remove the flatlands from
the Hillside ordinance and move the Hillside restriction line to the toe of the hills.
We have also embarked upon an exciting new program for providing
Short Term Care and Rehabilitative Services on an unused floor at our Lorber
Long Term Care Facility in Union City. This new program, in partnership with a
local health care system, will provide short term care to our residents, our members
and the community. This will allow us to develop the specialization needed to
be a leader in providing rehabilitative services. This program will be open to
all Masons and their families throughout the state and will provide neurological,
cardiac and orthopedic rehab.
This year, we began the implementation of a Person Centered Care
approach. This cultural change has and will continue to impact the way services
are provided to our residents and clients. Based upon our Masonic Values, this
program has already brought about change at both or our campuses, from simple
changes in the dining experience to more dramatic changes in providing more
resident friendly spaces for socialization and fellowship.

270

Proceedings of the

This has also been a great year for our existing programs. For the first
time, our Lorber Skilled Nursing Facility in Union City was awarded a 5 Star
Rating from Nursing Home Compare, the Medicare Rating System. This is the
highest rating that is reserved for the top 10 percent of nursing homes in the
United States. This year, we also had a zero deficiency survey. Less than 2% of
the nursing homes nationwide have achieved that distinction.
All of our programs strive to meet the Mission and Vision of the Masonic
Homes and we are very proud of all of our staff in embracing this Mission and
providing excellent care and services to our Brethren and their families.
CHILDREN’S SERVICES- Family Resource Center
The Masonic Homes Transition Program was created as an extension
of care and support serving those children, who resided at the Masonic Homes,
at the time of its closure in 2009. The Masonic Homes commitment toward their
care ensured that each child had a safe and successful transition plan. Each child
and their family were assigned a care manager, who worked with them to create
safe and stable living environments that would also meet their child’s educational
needs. Through financial support and assisting families access and apply for
public benefits and low-cost programs, the children continued on their path of
success that was established during their residency at the Masonic Homes.
During the 2013-2014 school year, the Transition Program served the 4
remaining children and their families. Of these 4 children, 2 children graduated
from high school in June 2014 and will start college this fall. They have also earned
a scholarship through the Masonic Homes Scholarship Program. Another child
emancipated and is living independently. And our last child will be a high school
senior next year and will continue to be served through the Transition Program.
The enduring support from the Masonic Homes has provided the children needed
stability and guidance which has allowed them to fulfill their childhood dreams.
The Masonic Homes Scholarship Program continues to offer scholarships
to alumni of the former Children’s Program. Scholarships are provided for up to
5 years toward undergraduate studies; up to 2 years toward Master’s programs;
and up to 5 years toward Doctoral programs. Additionally, scholars are able to
attend schools of their choice throughout the United States. The scholars receive
scholarships based on the type of school and their full-time or part-time status. A
hallmark of this program’s success has been the case management support that
is provided to ensure students access school support services, and successfully
navigate through college on their way to becoming independent adults. All scholars
must maintain a GPA requirement and re-apply for scholarship annually. This has
led to strengthening the students’ accountability for their own performance and
commitment toward their education.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

271

During the 2013-2014 school year, the scholarship program served a
total of 15 students. We had 3 students attending graduate school this past year,
1 working toward their doctorate degree and 2 working toward their master’s
degree. The remaining 12 scholars attended a variety of State Universities,
community colleges and a trade school in pursuit of their bachelor’s degree. For
the upcoming 2014-2015 school year, the Scholarship Program has approved a
total of 23 students to receive scholarships. It’s clear that our former children
alumni are on the right path, pursuing higher education and their dreams, with the
support from the Masonic Homes.
MASONIC FAMILY OUTREACH SERVICES – Family Resource Center
The Masonic Family Outreach Services (MFOS) program began in
October 2009, in response to the economic downturn and the overwhelming need
for support to our younger members, under the age of 60. Currently, the program
provides Information and Referrals through the Masonic Assistance line at 888466-3642. The Masonic Assistance line provides information-referrals to all
callers in need of community resources. We are able to serve callers with a wide
range of needs and across different age groups.
The MFOS program also provides Care Management services, which
are flexible and able to serve families in their own communities. This support
entails identifying resources for families struggling with today’s complex issues
and assisting them with applying for public benefits and other programs. Our
Care Managers provide hands-on support that best meets the member’s individual
needs. Care management support is extended to the entire Masonic family, with
no eligibility requirements or time limits.
Finally, the MFOS program can provide one-time financial assistance, in
which there are eligibility requirements and criteria goals that must be met. The
one-time financial assistance is provided only when it can serve as a bridge from
economic hardship toward self-sufficiency. An identified and agreed upon care
plan, about how to reach self-sufficiency, is the lynchpin to the success of this
program. All financial clients agree to partner with their Care Manager toward this
goal and must also apply and access any public benefits for which they qualify.
This past year a total of 27 clients were provided with direct financial
assistance and another 41 clients received on-going case management. The total
number served was 68 clients.

MASONIC SENIOR OUTREACH SERVICES
The Masonic Senior Outreach Services program (MSOS) experienced
significant growth since 2009 but has seemed to stabilize during the past two
years, as members and our lodges are more knowledgeable about services offered
through this program. Over this past year, we served on average 167 members
per month financially and an average of 68 members per month non-financially.
The MSOS program serves our elderly brethren and their wives and
widows who experience on-going economic difficulties related to living longer
than planned and to their increasing care costs. We are also serving younger
seniors who have had to seek early retirement due to loss of employment and
health related issues. This year a total of 307 clients were served, in which 241
clients received direct financial assistance and 66 clients received ongoing case
management. It is through the generous support of Masons, who give to the
Annual Fund and through planned giving, that ensures we are always in a position
to the meet the increasing and diverse needs of our most vulnerable members.
Finally, the MSOS Program made great strides this year with its
quarterly newsletter called the MSOS Gazette. The newsletter features department
highlights, exciting news about our clients, updates about outstanding lodge
partnerships, as well as trivia and health related articles. We hope that the MSOS
Gazette has strengthened a sense of “extended community” for our clients, their
families and lodges. Additionally, all of our MSOS financial clients with assets
and the ability to repay the program are now receiving financial statements
summarizing their Masonic Assistance support. These comprehensive reports
will allow easy repayment, when members are ready and able to do so. Through
repayment, the MSOS Program is able to preserve charitable dollars and extend
support to future members in need.
The Masonic Assistance line 888-466-3642, as the single point of inquiry
for all Masonic Assistance Programs, has made it easier for callers to obtain
information about any of our programs. The Masonic Assistance line telephone
number is printed on the new dues cards, so that it is readily available. During this
past year, the Masonic Assistance office has launched a satisfaction survey for
those applying for services. The feedback provided from the surveys has allowed
us to make process improvements and maintain excellent customer services to our
members. Moreover, the Masonic Assistance line has handled 1,691 calls just for
Information and Referrals alone.
Finally the Masonic Assistance office has worked closely with Grand
Lodge Member Services by providing needed outreach tools, program information
and guidance on “how to do outreach” toward their members, especially those
with remitted dues. The Remitted Dues Project was launched in June 2014 as a
collaborative effort to meet the needs of our members and bring them back into
the support of their lodges, where applicable.

LODGE OUTREACH INITIATIVE
Together, Masonic Outreach Services and San Diego Division IX created
the Lodge Outreach Initiative which began in July 2011. This strategic initiative
has focused on strengthening our partnerships with our lodges by formalizing a
training program and developing outreach materials and tools, which are utilized
by our lodge leaders as they fulfill their fraternal obligation of providing relief to
their members and sweethearts.
San Diego Division IX created the role of Training Coordinators, who
serve as district trainers to the lodges. They actively partner with MOS, serving
as a liaison to their district. The Division IX Training Coordinators participate in
an annual all-day training at the Masonic Homes in Covina, where they receive
a training binder and actively participated in problem solving scenarios and
identifying appropriate plans of action. The all-day training provides the needed
information to do outreach as well as “how to” do outreach. Quarterly meetings
then follow within the division, as the Training Coordinators network, problemsolve and support each other, ultimately strengthening the “safety net of relief”
for their members.
This past year, Division IX has focused their outreach efforts on how to
organize and facilitate relief projects, where groups of Masons, their wives and
Youth Orders can gather their efforts toward the good of a single objective. The
plan is to formalize best practices regarding all outreach efforts at the lodge level.
Finally, the Lodge Outreach Initiative was extended to Division II this
past year. Division II has embraced this partnership with MOS, as they too desired
to improve their outreach efforts. Division II Training Coordinators completed
their initial all-day training at the Masonic Homes in Union City and have held
their first quarterly meeting. The district Training Coordinators are now well
informed about the programs and services offered through Masonic Assistance
and are ready to go back and train the lodge leaders within their district.
By further testing the success of this initiative in another division, it
will allow MOS to refine the current training model with the intent to extend
the Lode Outreach Initiative to the rest of the fraternity. Expanding our outreach
efforts have positively impacted the number of members we serve. Together, our
collaborative and innovative work will better position us to meet the needs and
interests of our members, across the generational spectrum.

while partnering with staff to define what quality of life means to each individual.

Activity and Programing
As a resident-centered, mission-driven community, and in keeping
with the tenets of Free Masonry, the Masonic Homes of California promotes the
quality of life by empowering our members, their families and our community to
live well, and have active, meaningful and rewarding lives.
Staff has been challenged this past year with the significant differences
in the resident age groups. Listening to Frank Sinatra one day and switching to the
Beatles the next has been a different culture for staff.
This is the third year that we have partnered with Mt. San Antonio
College’s Older Adult Program to provide a “Brain Fitness” class for our
residents and seniors in our community. Mt. San Antonio College has teamed
with San Diego State University, California Community College, Educators of
Older Adults and a neuro–scientific software company to offer this Brain Fitness
Program. This program has proven successful in empowering cognitive functions
of seniors through participation in scientifically designed computer delivered brain
exercises, which will improve processing speed information, vision, hearing, both
long and short term memory and reaction time. Twelve residents attended this
class and feel they have improved in all these areas. The Brain Fitness class has
been such a success the classes have been expanded to 3 classes per week this
past year.
Fifty seniors from Mt. San Antonio College along with our residents
attended the summer swimming exercise classes that were held on campus.
On June 8, 2014, our campus enjoyed our 10th successful “Summer
Festival”. The Summer Festival joins together our Masonic Lodges and Eastern
Star. The Grand Master’s Summer Festival theme for the event was “Cat in the
Hat”. Over 300 guests were in attendance.

MASONIC HOMES UNION CITY

(seventy-nine), Life on campus begins with Independent Living (approximately

services available at Masonic homes at Union City through the Transitions
Department. The Coordinator sets up campus visits, conducts tours and
introductions and guides Masons and their families through the entire move-in
process and beyond. There are currently 2 vacant apartments and assessments
are in progress. The internal and external waiting lists are reviewed monthly or
as needed.
“Welcome Home” baskets for our new residents have been upgraded,
with input from our Resident- driven Welcome Committee to ensure the new
comers’ first few days are pleasant and the “basics” are on hand.
As the movement to electronic record keeping extends to all aspects of
documentation, a new scanning project is under way with the help of volunteers,
to get the entire master file archives into our electronic health record system for
safe retention, ease of access and reduction of paper.
Our Transitions Coordinator is collaborating with MOS staff to update the
Financial Summary for applicants and adding information on MediCal eligibility,
Power of Attorney, and comprehensive Medicare A, B and D information. Reports
are generated monthly to inform the RCFE Administrator and other departments
when residents level of care and financial status changes become evident.
Memory care is provided in the Traditions neighborhood, a delayed
egress unit with the capacity for 16 residents. An extensive remodeling project
was completed this year. The Garden adjacent to Traditions and shared with
Lorber residents was refreshed with the services of a Horticultural Therapist
who engaged residents in the process and with the addition of sturdy hotel-grade
outdoor furniture.
The most current focus is on staff training enhancements. Nationally
recognized memory care programming expert, Nancy Schier-Anselmo is
collaborating with our staff and spent a day at Union City in program review and
staff training in early September.
A multi-disciplinary team is reviewing out-placed residents and
determining how to best serve residents with difficult behavioral issues by
enhancements to on-campus services.
An alliance with the speech therapy graduate school of the University of
California, East Bay has been renewed and students about to graduate will, under
the direction of their professor, be conducting assessments and interacting with
the residents in Traditions for several days this fall.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

277

Memory Care is not just limited to Traditions. Our campus- wide
“Stepping Stones Program” is being launched this year. This “four-tiered”
approach to memory enhancement and memory care support begins at the lowest
level of care and seeks to provide individualized approaches for each resident.
Excluding our twenty-four Lorber residents and fifteen residents in Traditions,
our staff is currently tracking forty-one residents with very early or mild signs
of memory loss who, with a little additional support, can function well in their
current Assisted Living residence.
The Administrators for Covina and Union City met with Ms. SchierAnselmo to discuss options for incorporating “day-care” programming. Beginning
with identification (approximately twenty-two residents at Union City and ten at
Covina), the residents can be well served with guided integration into existing
active living programs and community-based programs such as P.A.C.E.- On Lok.
We have also begun discussions with a nationally recognized expert in
the area of “brain fitness”. Founder of the “Brain Emporium”, Associate Professor
of Psychology at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio, T.J. McCallum, PhD
is doing research in brain “exercise” programs, including computer software
programing, tactile and interactive gaming, and study to enhance and preserve
memory function for seniors. Professor McCallum will be visiting the Union
City campus in mid-October. A campus location has been identified to house the
Union City “Brain Emporium” and residents will have access to the new program
before the end of the year.
Social Services at Union City maintains full compliance with Title 22
Regulations regarding service plans and, in conjunction with an interdisciplinary
team which includes RCFE Health Management, Social Services, Dietary, and
Active Living, manages a comprehensive schedule for continuing review and
updates. Level of Care assessment and Service Planning documentation are on
track to become part of the Electronic Medical Record by mid-September.
Social Services and health teams, under the direction of a medical
doctor, successfully addressed several urgent and emergency mental health and
psychiatric issues. Team responses were professional, organized, timely, and
demonstrated the cohesiveness and expertise of current staff.
Volunteers are used more efficiently to address more resident needs
including a volunteer dedicated to the Low Vision Support Group, and a volunteer
who coordinated a very successful hospice meet-and-greet where residents and
staff became more familiar with hospice care providers in the Tri-City area.
Resident Health Care at Union City has benefited from the addition of
a new RCFE Administrator and RCFE Health Manager this spring. All systems
are in concurrent review and incremental “adjustments” to solid practices are
being incorporated to move this level of service to “best practice” status and
care standards. To that end, the Director of Quality Management, is chairing an

278

Proceedings of the

interdisciplinary Fall Prevention Task Force with the working mission to reduce
the number of falls and falls with injury. Extensive review and analysis have been
completed and interventions and action plans are being implemented.
More efficient staffing with less use of outside resources continues to be
a priority. New scheduling practices are in development.
At the heart of “Town Center” of the Union City Campus is the Medical
Office. The seasoned staff ensure all physicians reports are up-to-date and a new
system is in place to track due dates to ensure compliance. Annual required exams
such as eye exams, dental exams, and pacemaker checks are completed year
to date.
The RCFE Administrator, General Counsel, and Controller are currently
reviewing all physician contracts to create standardization and allow for
expansion of specialized services which can be offered on-site, including a focus
on preventive and holistic approaches such as acupuncture when ordered by a
physician and covered under Medicare.
We are also working with our Architectural design firm on changes to
the Medical Clinic. Once plans have been approved by the State, we will begin
remodeling the space to become a more inviting environment for our residents.
CHILD AND FAMILY SERVICES
Masonic Center for Youth and Families
Established in 2011, the Masonic Center for Youth and Families
(MCYAF) recently completed its third year of operation, diagnosing and treating
children and youth with learning, emotional, and behavioral difficulties. MCYAF
offers a unique and comprehensive, or “integrative”, method to combine the
different disciplines that treat children into one diagnostic and treatment regime
with the hope that it will identify all of the issues impacting the child.
MCYAF is on track to complete 60 assessments in 2014 and, in addition,
will provide treatment to over 350 total clients including “primary” (child) clients
and family members. As of September 2014, MCYAF is able to accommodate
new client assessments within a week and constantly strives to maintain this level
of access. During 2014 MCYAF has engaged in a review of how it measures
and reports client activity and is expanding its reporting in order to better track
the various services it provides and understand trends in each of the services.
Another area of enhanced focus is on reporting of clients who complete an
assessment at MCYAF and, for a variety of reasons, are not treated at MCYAF.
The new measures, which will be presented to the Board in October 2014, better
distinguish between assessment clients, client treatments and treatments provided
to family members.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

279

In addition to having a positive impact on the lives of children and
families, MCYAF actively seeks opportunities to raise awareness of the benefits
of an integrative approach. To that end, a group of MCYAF clinical providers
is applying to a national annual conference (American Psychological Assoc.
Division 39) to be held April 22-26, 2015 in San Francisco and for an international
bi-annual conference (International Psychoanalytic Assoc.) to be held July 22-25,
2015 in Boston to propose a panel presentation of an MCYAF Multiple Therapies
Case in ongoing treatment.

foundation for the future. It has been a pleasure and an honor to serve with the

Proceedings of the

Report of the Directors of the
Acacia Creek Retirement Community
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&A.M. of California:
Acacia Creek, our continuing care retirement community located
adjacent to the Masonic Home at Union City, is now completing its fourth year of
operation. I am pleased to report to you that we continue to grow our occupancy.
At the time of the last Annual Communication our occupancy was at 68%. Today
we are at 82% occupancy with additional move-ins scheduled. Due to our success
we were able to pay back $587,000 to Masonic Homes for its initial outlays to
Acacia Creek. Our goal is to reach stability in the coming year as we begin to
make payments on our debt as well as on the loan from Masonic Homes.
The revamped Marketing Program has resulted in deposits and moveins consistently, since its inception in the beginning of the fiscal year 2012. A
second duplex cottage is under construction and has been reserved --- another
positive indicator of the community’s progress. Based on the current numbers,
we have applied for our permanent Certificate of Occupancy from the California
Department of Social Services, another significant milestone.
Current residents’ satisfaction and happiness is apparent to prospective
buyers, and because of this our residents continue to be our best salespeople in
the community and are always involved in the sales process. Residents invite
friends and lodge brothers to join them for meals or for an overnight stay in the
guest apartments, and “host” them for dinner and entertainment, often resulting
in a new deposit.
Masterpiece Living is a national program of physical and mental
wellness which has been adopted by Acacia Creek. Measured against the national
benchmarks for residents in similar communities, our residents again this year
showed a lower level of physical problems and a higher level of nutritional and
physical activity.
The absorption of non-Masons into the Acacia Creek community has
been rewarding for the Fraternity. There is great camaraderie among them and
the community has been strengthened by adding to the mix. Three new residents
have become Master Masons, totaling eight new Master Masons from Acacia
Creek since opening, and more are expected to petition for degrees in the future.
Members of Acacia Creek are actively involved with Siminoff Daylight Lodge at
the Masonic Home at Union City, as members, officers, and in the construction of
the new outdoor degree site on the property.
The Acacia Creek staff continues to share feedback about the positive
work environment they enjoy through the team management concept that was
introduced last year. Employees are decision makers and feel a sense of ownership
in the operations of Acacia Creek. This results in a very low turnover among staff
adding to the comfort level of the residents.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

293

When the fraternity planned the Acacia Creek community, we envisioned
that it would include all levels of health care, including independent and assisted
living, skilled nursing, and memory care. To fulfill this goal, Acacia Creek has
worked with the Masonic Homes in designing the renovation of the Traditions
Program of the Masonic Home at Union City, the conversion of a floor in the
Lorber Building for specialized care for those with Dementia and acute health
care needs as well as a state of the art short term rehab floor for both Acacia Creek
and Masonic Homes residents.
A historic first joint meeting of the Acacia Creek and Masonic Homes
Board was held in February. This event brought together the two boards to review
and discuss joint strategic initiatives concerning both entities. Topics discussed
involved the improvements and new facilities on the Union City campus mentioned
above as well as the development of a Master Plan for all of the Masonic Homes
holdings. Additional discussion was held about methods of serving the needs of
our prospective clients over the long term and further improving the lives of our
current residents.
The Board wishes to extend our sincere appreciation to Chuck Major,
Executive Vice President of Acacia Creek, who is the heart and soul of the
management team and has been responsible for the high level of morale and
accountability of the staff and the strategic Marketing Program that has been
so successful.
I want to thank the members of the Grand Lodge Executive Committee,
the Grand Lodge staff, the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees, and the Acacia
Creek Board for their expertise, their vision, and their passion. Together we
look forward to continuing the mission of bringing Acacia Creek to stability and
financial security.
Respectfully submitted,

Proceedings of the

Report of the Trustees of the
California Masonic Foundation
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&A.M. of California:
Your California Masonic Foundation focused this year on evolving
our literacy and Investment in Success programs to reach a wider target population
of students in our communities and to make an even more profound difference
in California public education. Our programs continue to be aligned with the
Strategic Plan of the Masons of California and fully supported by the Grand
Lodge Executive Committee. We have increased the visibility of the Fraternity
in our communities and involved larger numbers of our members through the
Public Schools Advisory Councils. We continue to oversee a wide range of
programs supporting various needs within the Jurisdiction.
Strategic Initiatives
Once again, considerable progress was made this year in furthering the
two strategic initiatives the Foundation is responsible for - support to public
education and increasing Lodge involvement in the community. Our seven Public
Schools Advisory Councils continued their strong leadership by organizing and
conducting six Public Schools Month Kickoff celebrations in March and April,
2014, attended by over 800 Masons, community leaders, teachers, parents
and students. As a part of these events, the Foundation donated $712,000
to support Raising a Reader in K-3 classrooms and needed scholarships for
deserving high school students. These very successful celebrations further raised
community awareness of Freemasonry and demonstrated our dedication to both
public education and the lifelong learning of our students.
We have evolved our efforts based on our recognition that the role
of families and support networks plays an important part in a student’s
ability to succeed. Whether they are elementary school children or high school
students – the support from those around them can make all the difference. To
that end, we have engaged in partnerships, developed programs and encouraged
our brethren to bring families and communities together to support our schools.
We have identified key entry points in a child’s academic career in an effort
to affect the greatest change by leveraging our resources appropriately.
Literacy
This year we completed the third term of our ground breaking partnership
with the leader in child literacy programs - Raising a Reader. This nationally
recognized program provides children with books and the support necessary

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

295

to develop the reading and learning skills that will allow them to succeed
academically. But more importantly, the program focuses on the shared reading
experience between parent and child, encouraging family level engagement, to
strengthen family ties, eliminate achievement gaps, and transforms the student’s
learning experience. We are pleased to report that we have met our commitment
of raising $1.2 million over the three year period.
Thanks to this generosity by the Masons of California, Raising a Reader
will be fully installed in 400 California classrooms most at risk of academic
failure. One hundred high quality, professionally chosen books will continue to
be distributed to each family every year. And, by 2020, the Masons of California
will have affected the lives of more than 50,000 children and their families. The
Fraternity has received positive feedback from parents and educators across the
state, thus increasing public awareness of Freemasonry as a force for good in
our communities. Our impact will be felt for generations.
In addition, the grant received last year from the prestigious Anne E. Casey
Foundation, the organization that works with disadvantaged children, has allowed
research to begin on the effects of this integrated literacy/family engagement
model. The Foundation expects to begin seeing measurable data next year on the
effectiveness and impact of Raising a Reader.
The Foundation expresses its gratitude to Most Worshipful Cooper
and the Executive Committee for their committed leadership in continuing to
support Raising a Reader as the Grand Master’s and the Fraternity’s project.
This allows continuity and greater potential of making a profound and lasting
impact on literacy in this jurisdiction.
Investment in Success
The goal of the Foundation is that every dollar invested in a student’s
future has the potential to change a life forever. Investment in Success, now
completing its fourth year, has been our answer to this challenge. This year, 90
young people received a scholarship from the Foundation that few of them ever
dreamed possible. The scholarship dollars we continue to invest will change the
lives of the nearly 300 students currently enrolled in our program.
Investment in Success scholarships are awarded to students attempting
to overcome many of life’s challenges and obstacles to achieve their academic
dreams. Nearly all are first-in-family to college, have little or no resources– yet
all have demonstrated a powerful desire to succeed, a vision for their future,
and the commitment to better themselves and to give back to their communities.
To address these issues, the Foundation continues to include opportunities
for summer or third year courses to increase their chances of graduating
and potentially moving on into a four year school. In addition, our ongoing

296

Proceedings of the

partnership with the GLOW Foundation has ensured that our Investment in
Success students enter College Success programs and similar organizations that
offer financial aid, academic advising, and specialized support services – thus
increasing their chances of graduation and success.
Currently, our resources can only reach a limited number of deserving
students, yet each year millions of state financial aid dollars are left unclaimed
by students. To address this situation and allow more students to access these
funds, the Foundation partnered last year with GLOW and the College Access
Foundation of California to create “College Gold Rush,” a one-stop shop for
accessing financial aid resources and information usable by parents, students
and school administrators. Our experience with the site this year has yielded
several lessons learned that we will use to evolve and improve its effectiveness
next year.
Public Schools Advisory Councils
The Foundation recognizes that none of these accomplishments would
be possible without the support of our brethren. A few years ago, we created
Public Schools Advisory Councils, now in seven metropolitan areas around our
state. More than 90 of our brethren are members of these Councils. They are
the “boots on the ground” in our efforts to connect our work to education and
community leaders, families and students.
This March and April, more than 800 Masons, education leaders,
teachers, parents and students attended six Public Schools Month Kick Off
events statewide. Over 160 Masons attended, including members of the
Executive Committee and Foundation Trustees. During these events, which
were held at schools in school districts, we highlighted our support for public
education; thanked district leaders, teachers and parents for their important
roles; and presented a total of $712,000 to support Raising a Reader and Investment
in Success in these communities.
Each Council performed admirably and worked closely with the Grand
Lodge staff to assure successful Kick Off events. The Councils worked together
with their local school districts and GLOW to conduct the scholarship interview
and selection process. Personal presentations of the scholarship awards were
made where possible to further highlight the students’ accomplishments while
publicly reinforcing the Fraternity’s commitment to public education. Council
members also visited Lodges to make presentations about Raising a Reader and
seeking monetary support for the Fraternity’s project.
The Foundation Board of Trustees thanks each member of our Public
Schools Advisory Councils. You are critical to our success, whether you are
raising funds, interviewing students or planning an event - you are the keys to
our success. We are humbled by, and proud of, your tireless efforts on behalf of
the Foundation.

Teacher of the Year
The Foundation continued its major sponsorship this year of the
California Teacher of the Year program. The annual state banquet was held in
Sacramento in February and the five Teacher of the Year finalists were celebrated.
Your Grand Master and the Foundation were present and the Masons of
California were recognized for their strong support as a major sponsor for twenty
years. Most Worshipful Cooper gave remarks and presented our monetary gift to
each of the five finalists. The five were also honored at a celebration within their
own communities and received special gifts from the Foundation.
Other Programs
The Foundation continued this year to underwrite our existing leadership
development, Lodge growth and Masonic education programs; including the
Master and Wardens Leadership Retreats, Lodge Certification Program, Inspector
Development Academy, Masonic Formation, the Institute for Masonic Studies
and the Masonic Symposium. In addition, our Heritage sites, historic article
preservation, Library and Museum, and CMMT maintenance were funded, as
well as the Columbia historical museum project.
Board Governance
The Board of Trustees continued to function within the governance model
adopted two years ago across all the major boards and committees. This year
the Foundation was comfortable with the operations and reporting requirements
of the model and moved more into the longer term strategic planning discussion
encompassed by the Ends policies of the Board. The Board also held its annual
strategic planning retreat and focused on future Ends policy definition.
The Board continued to function smoothly in the governance model
thanks to the concerted efforts of Brad Colby, Director of Administration and
Governance, and the Board thanks him for the countless hours spent in keeping
us organized and on track.
Looking Forward to 2015
The Foundation will enter next year with its strategic initiatives progressing
well and making an ever increasing impact on public education. We will continue
to monitor the classrooms receiving Raising a Reader and involve even more of
our Lodge members in the activities of the Public Schools Advisory Councils.
We will further refine our Investment in Success program and improve the
College Gold Rush website to increase the number of students with whom

Report of the Board of Trustees

of the California Masonic Memorial Temple

Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge:
The Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple
(CMMT) respectfully submits its 59th annual report, summarizing its activity
during the 2013-2014 Masonic year. Those interested in more detailed
information are referred to the minutes of the meetings of the Board of Trustees
reposed in the archives of our Grand Lodge. Full and audited financial
statements are not included in this report, but are included in the appendices of
these proceedings.
The Board of Trustees is entrusted with the preservation, maintenance, and
future viability of the landmark CMMT facility that inspires and services our
members. The CMMT owns this magnificent edifice and derives its revenue
by leasing space to the Grand Lodge of California, whose offices are on the
third floor; to the Nob Hill Masonic Center that operates the garage and the
telecommunications facility on the roof; and to other third parties, primarily
Live Nation, who lease space in the building. We also receive tax-exempt
contributions from candidates who are initiated into our California lodges.
This year the facility celebrates its 56th year located at 1111 California
Street in San Francisco. The marble clad Temple continues to gain recognition as
a resource for cultural and social events. From the time of its opening to the
present day, it has served not only as a facility for Masonic gatherings, but also as
a venue for concerts and other events enjoyed by the greater community. The
auditorium is the second largest event space in the City of San Francisco and
currently hosts up to 54 concerts and 25 cultural or comedy events per year.
Over the past six years we have worked with Live Nation to bring better
efficiency in the rental of our building and to enhance its future viability. This
has been a long process involving negotiations with governmental agencies
as well as community interests. Needed renovations started in January and, as
deemed prudent for a project this size, we retained an owner’s construction
representative to protect our interests. Weekly meetings were held to monitor the
progress and address any issues that might arise. In addition to the renovations,
our five-year capital plan is being followed with repairs to the roof, parapet
wall, and terrazzo tile completed. We hope you are pleased with the results and
enjoy the enhancements that have been made to keep the building an attractive
destination and to enhance its role as a multipurpose venue.
At the time this report is being written, designs are being made for a new
centerpiece staircase to the main stage. This staircase will be exclusively used
at the Annual Communication and will be constructed of wood pieces collected

300

Proceedings of the

from all over the State of California – in a similar manner to which the twostory endomosaic mural in our foyer included natural material from all parts of
our jurisdiction.
As a result of our continued outreach, we have noticed further significant
improvements in our relationship with the community. Our Executive Vice
President Allan Casalou was invited to help plan the Nob Hill Association annual
fundraiser at the Fairmont Hotel, which included the tree lighting ceremony at
Huntington Park. We hope to be able to hold the fundraising event here at some
time in the future. CMMT, in conjunction with Live Nation, is making ongoing
contributions in support of the new Huntington Park Preservation Fund. While you
are visiting, we encourage you to walk around and enjoy the park, which is
located across California Street, in front of Grace Cathedral. Live Nation is
also offering reduced rental rates for ethnic and cultural performers, enhancing
Nob Hill’s reputation as a distinguished destination for patrons. We are hopeful
that our continued outreach will make our neighbors aware of the value our
building and fraternity offer to the surrounding community.
In addition to arrangements with Live Nation, CMMT receives
income from the Nob Hill Masonic Center (overseeing the parking facilities);
we also continue to host several cell towers on the building roof to generate
additional revenue.
The Board wishes to extend its gratitude to our Executive Vice President
and Grand Secretary Allan Casalou, our Chief Financial Officer Thomas J. Boyer,
and Brad Colby, director of administration and board governance, as well as
their respective staff who work so diligently in representing our interests, and
maintaining and managing the building. We also thank the grand master, Most
Worshipful John L. Cooper for the opportunity to serve, and for his support and
faith in our efforts.
Respectfully submitted,

Report of the Board of Directors

of the Nob Hill Masonic Center, Inc.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Nob Hill Masonic Center, Inc. is unique among the various Masonicentity boards in California in that it is our only for profit, income tax paying entity
responsible for overseeing the efficient and profitable operations of the garage
located within the California Masonic Memorial Temple building at the top of
Nob Hill. One of our most important responsibilities is to ensure payment of a
dividend to our Grand Lodge each fiscal year. This dividend helps fund the many
ways in which the California Masons make a profound difference in the lives of
our members and in our communities. I am proud to announce that Fiscal Year
2012/2013 was the best year ever for the Nob Hill Masonic Center and that the
dividend it will provide to our Grand Lodge is also the largest to date. The current
dividend to the Grand Lodge provides approximately a $4.00 offset for cost of
per capita.
To continue this level of success and to ensure the efficient and safe
management of our garage, we have continued our engagement with ACE Parking.
ACE is one of the City’s most recognized garage operators and has managed the
day-to-day operations of the facility well. Sustainment of the monthly parking and
daily parking growth will be the key to driving the business in this coming year.
With the California Masonic Memorial Temple being closed due to construction
starting in February 2014, these two aspects are critical. It is planned that once the
renovation is completed and events resume in September 2014, the facility will
be a strong draw for special events that will fuel the Event Parking and should
position us to realize the revenues that we are forecasting and the dividend that
meets our Ends Policy.
Additional sources of revenue that support the Nob Hill Masonic Center
include our continuation of our agreement with ZIP and Get Around cars to use
designated parking spaces in our garage. We also continued an agreement with
Suite America to use designated spaces in our garage for the corporate cars of
visiting corporate executives. Maximizing our parking space during events by
using valet program will also contribute to our continued growth and success.
All of these agreements and programs ensure a steady revenue stream and make
our location a growing hub for these car sharing services for people throughout
San Francisco.
The safety of our patrons is of the highest concern to the board. The
security firm, along with the improvements made to the surveillance and security
system implemented last year, help maintain the garage’s convenient and secure
24-hour access. The automation used to manage the access in and out of the garage
continues to prove itself valuable in keeping the labor expenses down.

fairly conservative view of the next six years predicts that the Nob Hill Masonic
Center will provide $2.2 million in dividends to our Grand Lodge, $600,000 to
charitable programs, another $500,000 in capital reserves/expenditures, and $1
million in retained earnings to cover 2 years of dividends plus $200,000. This
will allow the Nob Hill Masonic Center to consistently provide a substantial
dividend to our Grand Lodge and to also contribute to local and our fraternal

Proceedings of the
Report of the Committee
on Finance

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A.M. of California:
The California Masonic Code, Section 406.035 E, requires the Committee
on Finance to review all of the proposed Recommendations and Resolutions to
be considered at the Annual Communication and to report on the financial impact
these items may have on the Grand Lodge budget.
Earlier this year, the committee reviewed the Carry-Over Resolutions and
New Resolutions as provided by the Grand Secretary. On July 28, we finalized our
report on the cost impact of each item. The Grand Secretary on July 22 posted the
report, with the legislation, to the lodges. Only one resolution was found to have
any financial impact on the Grand Lodge, and in as much as our written report has
been distributed, I will report on it now and not later during the session.
Resolution No. 14-14 Adds a Grand Historian. The proponents of this
resolution seek to add the Grand Lodge Officer position of Grand Historian. The
Resolution requires the Grand Historian to assist in the preservation of artifacts
held by Grand Lodge, to travel through the state to assist individual lodges in
researching the lodge history and preserving lodge artifacts. The Grand Historian
is further obligated to write scholarly articles for publication and perform other
duties that might be assigned by the Grand Master.
Section 407.070 of the California Masonic Code requires the Grand
Lodge reimburse Grand Lodge Officers for their necessary, out of pocket expenses
in the performance of their duties. The Resolution does not mandate the amount
of travel the Grand Historian should undertake. This would likely be a decision
of the Grand Master who will have planned for such expenses as Deputy Grand
Master. For the purposes of this report, the Committee on Finance estimates the
Grand Master would budget between $500 and $750 per month for travel and
other necessary expenses of the Grand Historian, which includes attendance at the
Annual Communication. In addition there will be initial costs of regalia and other
items regularly provided to all Grand Lodge Officers.
It is therefore the opinion of the Committee on Finance that this
Resolution, if adopted, would add expenses to the Grand Lodge Budget in the
range of $6,000 to $9,000 per year. This is the maximum impact on the Grand
Lodge budget.
There are a number of Resolutions that would cause changes to the Ritual
or the Monitor. It has been a practice of the Grand Lodge to make the printed
changes and produce new ciphers and monitors only after the current inventory
has been depleted or simply make them available online. Therefore, there is no
additional expense caused by the adoption of these Resolutions.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

309

The Finance Committee also reviewed Grand Master’s Decision No.
1 and 2, and Recommendations Nos. 1 through 6. Neither the Grand Master’s
Decision nor any of the Grand Master’s Recommendations would have a financial
impact on the Grand Lodge budget.
To repeat, it is the view of the Committee on Finance, with the exception
of Resolution 14-14, that none of the other resolutions or the Grand Master’s
Decision or Recommendations will have a financial impact on the Grand
Lodge budget.

Eric E. Buril
Tony Garcia, Jr.

Proceedings of the
Report of the Committee

on Institute for Masonic Studies

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California
The Institute for Masonic Studies (IMS) continues to provide high
quality Masonic education events, materials and resources to the Masons of
California. These resources are also made available to the public who study and
appreciate the significant contributions the fraternity has made throughout history.
The members of the institute appreciate the confidence and faith reposed in them
by the Most Worshipful John L. Cooper, III, Grand Master, and the many brethren
who have supported the activities of the IMS this past year.
14th Annual California Masonic Symposium
The symposium continued the format, which was started in 2012, with
speakers presenting twice - once on Saturday, September 20, at the San Francisco
Scottish Rite Masonic Center with 91 in attendance, and then on Sunday, September
21, at the Pasadena Scottish Rite with 183 in attendance. Each day’s program was
identical. The symposium was sponsored by the Grand Lodge of California, the
California Masonic Foundation, and the Institute for Masonic Studies. The topic,
Freemasonry and the Creation of the American Republic, generated a renewed
interest in the historical origins of Freemasonry in America and its impact on the
formation of our government.
This is an overview and abstract for each presenter prepared by Most
Worshipful R. Stephen Doan, Past Grand Master and Vice Chair of the IMS:
The American Republic is a unique experiment in self-government,
whose roots are in part to be found in the Freemasonry of the 18th century.
The 14th Annual California Masonic Symposium will explore how this
experiment in self-government has evolved through the years since 1776,
and how Masonic principles have continued to guide its development
for almost 250 years. The presenters will show that Freemasonry has
influenced the course of self-government in several significant ways.
•

Dr. John Cooper, Grand Master of Masons in California, will
present a paper entitled Freemasonry and the Creation of the
Public Space. Arguing that self-government is not possible
without a place where ideas can be explored and discussed, he
will share research on how consensus is built in a democracy
through civil discourse. Freemasons of the 18th century were
pioneers in civil discourse, and what they discovered has had a
lasting influence on our form of government. Dr. Cooper is the
2014 Henry Wilson Coil Lecturer.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

311

•

R. Stephen Doan, Past Grand Master of Masons of California,
will present a paper entitled Freemasonry and the Progressive
Movement in California. California was an important
contributor to the Progressive Movement, and California
Freemasons were in key positions. This paper will consider the
goals of the Progressive Movement, who were the Freemasons
in key roles, how reforms of the Progressive Movement were
tried first in California’s Grand Lodge and how California
Freemasonry avoided the excesses of Progressivism, including
the impact which Progressivism has had on civil discourse.

•

William J. Miklos, Grand Marshal of the Grand Lodge of
California, will present a paper on the influence of Freemasonry
on the development of constitutionalism in America. The idea
of civil discourse within a framework of accepted rules was
another Masonic contribution to the creation and perpetuation
of the American Republic.

•

Kent Roberts, Director of the National Civility Center,
will present a paper on how the Civility Movement today is
essential to the survival of the American Republic. The Civility
Movement has discovered that Freemasons have principles,
which are in harmony with this movement, and Grand
Lodges are now considering a partnership with this emerging
commitment to civil discourse.

Each day, the symposium concluded with a panel discussion on the
symposium’s topic. The panel included all of the presenters and questions were
submitted during the break.
Henry Wilson Coil Library and Museum
Oversight of the Grand Lodge’s library and museum remains an
important part of the mission of the Institute for Masonic Studies. The library,
named for the celebrated Masonic scholar and California Mason, Henry Coil, is
a repository of the history and material culture of Freemasonry in California. The
Grand Secretary and his staff – primarily Worshipful Adam Kendall, Collections
Manager, manage the operation of the library and museum. Their efforts to
preserve, restore, and exhibit the holdings of the library and museum, make it one
of the leading institutions of its kind in the United States.
This past year we saw an increase in the amount of time Adam has
spent presenting at various conferences as well as the publication of his essays/
presentations. Please see the following library reports prepared by Worshipful
Adam Kendall. These reports have been compiled over the course of this Masonic
year commencing in October 2013 and concluding in October 2014.

the mystical trappings and overtures of secret and fraternal
societies. I will briefly describe the history of the romanticism

Basic Candidate Education Program

The institute released its revision and reformation of the Basic Candidate
Education program of the Grand Lodge during last year’s Annual Communication.
The new program is an enhanced and enriched online education experience for
Entered Apprentices, Fellow Crafts, and Master Masons. The program includes
opportunities to practice mastery of our ritual and reflect upon the teachings of
each degree. Outstanding artwork, video, and online links will be added to the
readings to provide more depth and breadth in the study of the three degrees of
Masonry. As of right now we have 1,864 members using this program.
The UCLA Project: Advancing the Study and
Understanding of Freemasonry
Since 2009, the Grand Lodge of California has partnered with the UCLA
History Department and Distinguished Professor of History, Dr. Margaret Jacob,
to lift the “veil of secrecy” that surrounds and obscures Freemasonry’s place in
history. Over the past four years, four undergraduate courses have been developed
and five scholars have been supported in their research, scholarship, and teaching.
These scholars continue to advance the study and understanding of Freemasonry
and its proper place in developing and continuing civil society. This past year,
Dr. Maria Eugenia Vazquez Semadini, received the sought after position of postdoctoral fellow supported by the partnership.
In April 2014, the Grand Lodge of California and the UCLA History
Department teamed to present the 3rd Annual International conference on
Freemasonry in Latin America. The conference brought together renowned
scholars and lecturers from North America and Europe. The presenters and their
papers were:
Stefan-Ludwig Hoffman, Ph.D. - Sacrifice and Sovereignty: German
Freemasonry and the Image of Mass Death before 1914 Hoffman is an
associate professor of late modern Europe at the University of California,
Berkeley. The author of several books, including, “The Politics of
Sociability: Freemasonry and German Civil Society” and “Civil Society:
1750-1914.” He specializes in the afterlife of Enlightenment ideas and
practices in the 19th century and transnational history of the tensions
between democracy and civil society.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

315

Lilith Mahmud, Ph.D. - Thanks to Mozart: Cultivation and Aesthetics
among Women Freemasons in Italy Mahmud is an assistant professor of
women’s studies and anthropology at the University of California, Irvine.
The author of “The Brotherhood of Freemason Sisters: Gender, Secrecy,
and Fraternity in Italian Masonic Lodges,” she specializes in feminist
anthropology and anthropology in Europe.
William D. Moore, Ph.D. - Solomon’s Temple in America: Masonic
Architecture, Popular Culture, and Biblical Imagery, 1865-1930 Moore is
an associate professor of American material culture at Boston University.
A widely referenced Masonic scholar, he is also the author of several
books and articles, including, “Masonic Temples: Freemasonry, Ritual
Architecture, and Masculine Archetypes,” and co-editor of “Secret
Societies in America: Foundational Studies of Fraternalism.”
Joy Porter, Ph.D. - Native American Indian Freemasonry: From Joseph
Brant to the 21st Century Porter is a professor of indigenous history at
the University of Hull in England. A widely referenced scholar, she is
also the organizer of two major international conferences and author of
several books and articles, including, “Native American Freemasonry:
Associationalism and Performance in America.” Porter is currently
writing “The American Indian Poet of the First World War: Fran ‘Toronto’
Prewett, 1892-1962.”
Over 205 scholars, students and Masons attended the conference held on
the campus of UCLA.

serve the craft and its brethren.
